questions.question: Human rights are best defined as:
choices: Standards that belong only to the nationals and citizens of a State, to the exclusion of visitors and migrants
Universally agreed basic standards which belong to everyone from the mere fact of being human and which aim to ensure that every person is treated with dignity and respect
Standards granted to individuals by their State through national legislation, which the State may therefore withdraw
Standards that apply only in States that have adopted a democratic political system
questions.explanation: Rights are inherent: they belong to everyone by virtue of being human. The State does not give people their rights, it must respect, protect and fulfil them.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Section 1 ; Plan I.A

questions.question: Which principle is described in the course as being 'at the centre of human rights' and as featuring in all the major human rights treaties?
choices: The principle of subsidiarity
The margin of appreciation
The principle of proportionality
The principle of non-discrimination
questions.explanation: Rights are inherent to all persons without discrimination and irrespective of the political system of the State. Subsidiarity, proportionality and the margin of appreciation are principles governing the Court's work, not the foundation of human rights as such.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Section 1 ; Plan I.A

questions.question: Under international law, States are obliged to respect, protect and fulfil human rights. 'To respect' means:
choices: That States must pass laws and create mechanisms to prevent violations by State authorities and non-State actors
That States must not interfere with or restrict human rights
That States must compensate anyone whose rights have been violated
That States must take positive action to ensure the enjoyment of human rights
questions.explanation: The triad is: respect = do not interfere; protect = legislate and create mechanisms against violations, including by private actors; fulfil = take positive action.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Role of the State ; Plan I.A

questions.question: Under international law, States are obliged to respect, protect and fulfil human rights. 'To protect' means:
choices: Refraining from any interference with the rights set out in the Convention
Defending the State's citizens before international courts
Taking positive action to ensure that everyone actually enjoys their rights
Passing laws and creating mechanisms to prevent violations of rights by State authorities AND by non-State actors
questions.explanation: The protection obligation covers violations committed by private (non-State) actors as well, which is why purely 'vertical' reasoning is insufficient.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Role of the State ; Plan I.A

questions.question: Under international law, States are obliged to respect, protect and fulfil human rights. 'To fulfil' means:
choices: That States must execute the judgments of the European Court of Human Rights
That States must ratify every additional protocol to the Convention
That States must abstain from restricting human rights
That States must take positive action to ensure the enjoyment of human rights
questions.explanation: 'Fulfil' is the proactive limb: creating the conditions in which rights become effective, not merely abstaining from violating them.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Role of the State ; Plan I.A

questions.question: The statement that human rights are 'interdependent and indivisible' means that:
choices: Every right protected by the Convention has exactly the same legal regime
All the rights are intertwined, so that the fact of not respecting one of them may adversely affect another
There must be a violation of at least two rights for an application to be lodged with the Court
Everyone is entitled to these rights in equal measure, without discrimination
questions.explanation: Interdependence and indivisibility describe the links between rights (non-observance of one may impact another). The wording about everyone being entitled to these rights in equal measure without discrimination describes universality and non-discrimination, a different idea. This is annales Question 5.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Glossary ; QCM ANGLAIS Q5

questions.question: Which of the following is classified in the course as a civil and political right rather than an economic, social and cultural right?
choices: The right to education
The right to join a trade union
The right not to be subjected to torture
The right to an adequate standard of living
questions.explanation: Civil and political: life, fair trial, freedom from torture. Economic, social and cultural: work, trade union, health, education, adequate standard of living.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Section 1 ; Plan I.A

questions.question: Which of the following is classified in the course as an economic, social and cultural right?
choices: The right not to be subjected to torture
The right to life
The right to a fair trial
The right to work
questions.explanation: Work, trade union membership, health, education and an adequate standard of living form the economic, social and cultural category.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Section 1 ; Plan I.A

questions.question: How many Member States does the Council of Europe currently have, according to the course?
questions.explanation: 46 since Russia ceased to be a member in 2022. Careful: the printed course handout (an older Irish document) still says 47, but the lecture notes and the course plan say 46. 27 and 28 are European Union figures.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Section 1 ; Plan I.B
questions.flag: The handout 'Guide for the Civil & Public Service' still says 47. The correct current figure is 46.

questions.question: How many Member States does the European Union currently have, according to the course?
questions.explanation: 27 since the United Kingdom left. 46 is the Council of Europe. The handout's figure of 28 predates Brexit.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Section 1 ; Plan I.B
questions.flag: The handout still says 28 (pre-Brexit).

questions.question: The primary human rights instrument of the Council of Europe is:
choices: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
The Vienna Declaration and Programme of Action
The European Union Charter of Fundamental Rights
The European Convention on Human Rights
questions.explanation: The Convention belongs to the Council of Europe. The Charter of Fundamental Rights belongs to the European Union.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Section 1 ; Plan I.B

questions.question: Rights are protected in the European Union by:
choices: The European Convention on Human Rights, enforced by the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg
The European Union Charter of Fundamental Rights, enforced by the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg
The European Convention on Human Rights, enforced by the Court of Justice of the European Union in Luxembourg
The European Union Charter of Fundamental Rights, enforced by the Court of Justice of the European Union in Luxembourg
questions.explanation: Two distinct systems: Convention/Strasbourg for the Council of Europe, Charter/Luxembourg for the European Union.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Section 1 ; Plan I.B

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the relationship between the Council of Europe and the European Union is correct?
choices: The two organisations share the same structure and working methods but have different courts
The two organisations have identical membership
Every Member State of the Council of Europe is also a Member State of the European Union, but the reverse is not true
Every Member State of the European Union is also a Member State of the Council of Europe, but the reverse is not true
questions.explanation: EU membership implies Council of Europe membership (46 vs 27). The two organisations are entirely separate in structure and working methods.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Section 1 ; Plan I.B

questions.question: Which of the following names is correct?
choices: European Convention ON Human Rights and European Court ON Human Rights
European Convention OF Human Rights and European Court OF Human Rights
European Convention ON Human Rights, but European Court OF Human Rights
European Convention OF Human Rights, but European Court ON Human Rights
questions.explanation: A classic trap flagged by the lecturer: Convention ON, Court OF.
questions.source: CM Anglais, opening ; Plan I.B (pièges de dénomination)

questions.question: What is the full official name of the ECHR?
choices: The European Convention for the Protection of Fundamental Rights and Public Freedoms
The European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms
The European Charter for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms
The European Treaty on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms
questions.explanation: Usually shortened to 'European Convention on Human Rights'.
questions.source: CM Anglais, opening ; Plan I.B

questions.question: The European Court of Human Rights sits in:
choices: Strasbourg
The Hague
Brussels
Luxembourg
questions.explanation: Strasbourg for the European Court of Human Rights; Luxembourg for the Court of Justice of the European Union.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Section 1 ; Plan I.B

questions.question: Where are human rights usually found in legal terms?
choices: In the case law of international courts alone, since no treaty can be exhaustive
In international or regional treaties, or in national constitutions and national legislation
Exclusively in United Nations treaties
Exclusively in the constitutions of democratic States
questions.explanation: They form a legal statement of universally accepted principles on how a State should treat everyone within its jurisdiction.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Section 1 ; Plan I.A

questions.question: According to the course, what is the classic shortcoming of most international and regional human rights instruments, which the ECHR avoids?
choices: They protect too few rights to be of practical use
They bind only the States that have ratified them
They can be derogated from in times of war
The rights they contain remain theoretical because the instrument is a mere declaration of intent, with no court before which individuals can directly enforce them
questions.explanation: The ECHR is considered the most successful regional instrument precisely because its rights are directly enforceable against States and individuals have a right of individual application.
questions.source: CM Anglais, The European Convention on Human Rights ; Plan II

questions.question: The European Convention on Human Rights was written in ... and came into force in ...
questions.explanation: Written 1950, in force 1953. 1948 is the Universal Declaration of Human Rights; 1959 is the year the Court itself was set up.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Section 2 ; Plan II

questions.question: Article 1 of the Convention concerns:
choices: The right to life
The obligation to respect human rights, requiring all parties to secure the Convention rights to everyone within their jurisdiction
The prohibition of discrimination
The right to an effective remedy
questions.explanation: Article 1 is the general obligation clause. Note that the Court sometimes expands the scope of the Convention by interpretation, finding rights not expressly stated.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Section 2 ; Plan II

questions.question: Who benefits from the rights contained in the Convention in a State party?
choices: Everyone within the State's jurisdiction, including visitors, migrant workers, asylum seekers and refugees
Only persons lawfully present on the territory of that State
Only nationals of States that are parties to the Convention
Only the nationals and citizens of that State
questions.explanation: Jurisdiction, not nationality, is the criterion. See Hirsi Jamaa and Others v Italy [2012], where migrants who were not Italian citizens were protected.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 1 ; Plan II

questions.question: In Hirsi Jamaa and Others v Italy [2012], the Court held that:
choices: The case was inadmissible because the applicants had not exhausted Italian domestic remedies
Italy could lawfully return the migrants because they were not Italian citizens
Convention rights apply even when a State operates outside its own territory, so migrants intercepted at sea and sent back to Libya fell within Italy's jurisdiction
Migrants intercepted on the high seas fall outside the jurisdiction of the intercepting State
questions.explanation: The case illustrates the extraterritorial reach of the Article 1 jurisdiction obligation.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 1

questions.question: The Vienna Declaration and Programme of Action of 1993 reaffirmed human rights as:
choices: Absolute, unqualified, inherent and inalienable
Universal, indivisible, interdependent and interrelated
Universal, enforceable, justiciable and binding
Civil, political, economic and social
questions.explanation: Underpinned by further principles such as dignity, respect, transparency, accessibility and foreseeability.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), end of Section 5

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed in the course among the principles underpinning human rights alongside universality and indivisibility?
choices: Reciprocity
Accessibility
Foreseeability
Dignity
questions.explanation: The course lists dignity, respect, transparency, accessibility and foreseeability. Reciprocity is alien to human rights logic: a State's obligations do not depend on other States performing theirs.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), end of Section 5

questions.question: The source document on which the course handout is based is:
choices: 'European Convention on Human Rights: Guide for the Civil & Public Service', Irish Human Rights Commission
The Council of Europe's official commentary on the Convention
A textbook published by the University of Montpellier
A guide published by the Registry of the European Court of Human Rights
questions.explanation: This explains why so many of the illustrative cases in the handout are Irish (Airey, Norris, Johnston, Keegan, DG).
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Source

questions.question: Which Convention article protects the right to life?
choices: Article 5
Article 1
Article 3
Article 2
questions.explanation: Art. 2 right to life; art. 3 prohibition of torture; art. 5 liberty and security; art. 1 general obligation.
questions.source: CM Anglais, list of articles ; Plan II.A

questions.question: Which Convention article prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment?
choices: Article 3
Article 7
Article 2
Article 4
questions.explanation: Article 3. The difference between torture and inhuman or degrading treatment is a matter of degree, assessed through the severity test.
questions.source: CM Anglais, list of articles ; Plan II.A

questions.question: Which Convention article prohibits slavery, servitude and forced labour?
choices: Article 3
Article 11
Article 4
Article 5
questions.explanation: Article 4.
questions.source: CM Anglais, list of articles ; Plan II.A

questions.question: Which Convention article protects the right to liberty and security, and therefore prohibits arbitrary detention?
choices: Article 2
Article 5
Article 6
Article 4
questions.explanation: Article 5. Article 6 is the fair trial, which comes after the question of detention.
questions.source: CM Anglais, list of articles ; Plan II.A

questions.question: Which Convention article protects the right to a fair trial?
choices: Article 5
Article 13
Article 7
Article 6
questions.explanation: Article 6, the most frequently invoked article before the Court. Do not confuse it with article 13 (effective remedy before a national authority).
questions.source: CM Anglais, list of articles ; Plan II.A

questions.question: Which Convention article lays down the principle 'no punishment without law'?
choices: Article 6
Article 7
Article 4
Article 5
questions.explanation: Article 7, which prohibits retroactive criminal law and retroactive aggravation of penalties.
questions.source: CM Anglais, list of articles ; Plan II.A

questions.question: Which Convention article protects the right to respect for private and family life?
choices: Article 10
Article 9
Article 8
Article 12
questions.explanation: Article 8, a qualified right.
questions.source: CM Anglais, list of articles ; Plan II.A

questions.question: Which Convention article protects freedom of thought, conscience and religion?
choices: Article 10
Article 9
Article 8
Article 11
questions.explanation: Article 9. Article 10 is freedom of expression, article 11 freedom of assembly and association.
questions.source: CM Anglais, list of articles ; Plan II.A

questions.question: Which Convention article protects freedom of expression?
choices: Article 8
Article 9
Article 11
Article 10
questions.explanation: Article 10.
questions.source: CM Anglais, list of articles ; Plan II.A

questions.question: Which Convention article protects freedom of assembly and association, including the right to form or join a trade union?
choices: Article 11
Article 12
Article 10
Article 9
questions.explanation: Article 11.
questions.source: CM Anglais, list of articles ; Plan II.A

questions.question: Which Convention article protects the right to marry?
choices: Article 8
Article 12
Article 14
Article 11
questions.explanation: Article 12.
questions.source: CM Anglais, list of articles ; Plan II.A

questions.question: Which Convention article protects the right to an effective remedy?
choices: Article 13
Article 5
Article 6
Article 14
questions.explanation: Article 13: the possibility to challenge a decision before a national authority, and that possibility must be effective.
questions.source: CM Anglais, list of articles ; Plan II.A

questions.question: Which Convention article prohibits discrimination?
choices: Article 1
Article 13
Article 12
Article 14
questions.explanation: Article 14, which is not a standalone right and must be pleaded together with another Convention right.
questions.source: CM Anglais, list of articles ; Plan II.A

questions.question: Which Convention article allows derogation in time of war or other public emergency?
choices: Article 1
Article 16
Article 15
Article 14
questions.explanation: Article 15. Some rights may never be derogated from, including freedom from torture, freedom from slavery and no punishment without law.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 15

questions.question: Article 16 of the Convention deals with:
choices: The prohibition of the abuse of rights
Derogation in time of emergency
Restrictions on the political activity of aliens
The obligation to furnish necessary facilities to the Court
questions.explanation: Article 16 concerns restrictions on the political activity of aliens. The course notes that there have been very few cases and no judgment to date finding a violation.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 16
questions.flag: The handout states that 'the government cannot restrict political activity simply because a person is not a citizen'. Article 16 in fact PERMITS such restrictions; it is the Court that reads the provision very narrowly (Piermont v France, 1995). Answer as taught, but do not repeat the handout's gloss in an essay.

questions.question: The protection of private property is guaranteed by:
choices: Article 1 of Protocol No. 7
Article 1 of Protocol No. 1
Article 1 of Protocol No. 4
Article 1 of the Convention
questions.explanation: Protocol 1, article 1. It does not mean that no one can be deprived of their property, but that deprivation must be provided for by law and, in principle, compensated.
questions.source: CM Anglais, protocols ; Plan II.B

questions.question: The right to education is guaranteed by:
choices: Article 14 of the Convention
Article 2 of Protocol No. 7
Article 3 of Protocol No. 1
Article 2 of Protocol No. 1
questions.explanation: P1-2. It also requires the State to respect the right of parents to ensure education does not conflict with their religious beliefs, which is the basis of Lautsi v Italy.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Protocol 1 ; Plan II.B

questions.question: The right to free elections is guaranteed by:
choices: Article 5 of Protocol No. 7
Article 3 of Protocol No. 1
Article 2 of Protocol No. 1
Article 3 of Protocol No. 4
questions.explanation: P1-3: States must hold free and secret elections.
questions.source: CM Anglais, protocols ; Plan II.B

questions.question: Which Protocol article abolishes the death penalty EXCEPT in specific circumstances such as times of war?
choices: Article 2 of the Convention
Article 1 of Protocol No. 4
Article 1 of Protocol No. 13
Article 1 of Protocol No. 6
questions.explanation: P6-1 abolishes the death penalty with exceptions (war, treason). P13-1 abolishes it in ALL circumstances. This distinction is a classic trap.
questions.source: CM Anglais, protocols ; Plan II.B
questions.flag: The course adds 'treason' to the Protocol 6 exceptions. Article 2 of Protocol 6 in fact covers only acts committed in time of war or of imminent threat of war. Answer as taught, but know the text.

questions.question: Which Protocol article abolishes the death penalty in ALL circumstances?
choices: Article 1 of Protocol No. 13
Article 1 of Protocol No. 6
Article 2 of the Convention
Article 1 of Protocol No. 7
questions.explanation: P13-1, with no exception for time of war. The course's illustration of the ratification rule is Turkey and Protocol 13.
questions.source: CM Anglais, protocols ; Plan II.B
questions.flag: The course says Turkey has not ratified Protocol 13. Turkey in fact ratified it on 20 February 2006 (in force 1 June 2006); today Azerbaijan is the only Council of Europe member not to have ratified it. The rule the example illustrates (a protocol binds only its ratifying States) remains correct.

questions.question: The right of appeal in criminal matters is guaranteed by:
choices: Article 2 of Protocol No. 7
Article 6 of the Convention
Article 4 of Protocol No. 7
Article 3 of Protocol No. 7
questions.explanation: P7-2. P7-3 is compensation for wrongful conviction and P7-4 is ne bis in idem.
questions.source: CM Anglais, protocols ; Plan II.B

questions.question: Compensation for wrongful conviction is guaranteed by:
choices: Article 4 of Protocol No. 7
Article 41 of the Convention
Article 3 of Protocol No. 7
Article 2 of Protocol No. 7
questions.explanation: P7-3. Article 41 is just satisfaction awarded by the Court itself, which is a different mechanism.
questions.source: CM Anglais, protocols ; Plan II.B

questions.question: The principle 'non bis in idem', the right not to be tried or punished twice for the same facts, is guaranteed by:
choices: Article 2 of Protocol No. 7
Article 7 of the Convention
Article 4 of Protocol No. 7
Article 5 of Protocol No. 7
questions.explanation: P7-4. Article 7 of the Convention deals with legality and non-retroactivity, which is a different matter.
questions.source: CM Anglais, protocols ; Plan II.B

questions.question: Equality between spouses is guaranteed by:
choices: Article 4 of Protocol No. 7
Article 5 of Protocol No. 7
Article 14 of the Convention
Article 12 of the Convention
questions.explanation: P7-5. Article 12 is the right to marry, article 14 is the prohibition of discrimination in the enjoyment of other Convention rights.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Protocol 7

questions.question: Which Protocol contains the prohibition of imprisonment for debt, freedom of movement, the prohibition of expulsion of nationals and the prohibition of collective expulsion of aliens?
choices: Protocol No. 4
Protocol No. 1
Protocol No. 7
Protocol No. 12
questions.explanation: Protocol 4, articles 1 to 4 respectively.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Protocol 4

questions.question: Protocol No. 12 concerns:
choices: The right to free elections
A general prohibition of discrimination, extending protection beyond the enjoyment of the other Convention rights
The abolition of the death penalty in all circumstances
The prohibition of collective expulsion of aliens
questions.explanation: Whereas article 14 is not autonomous, Protocol 12 creates a free-standing prohibition of discrimination.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Protocol 12 ; Article 14
questions.flag: The handout says Protocol 12 'will enter into force when ratified by ten Contracting States'. It in fact entered into force on 1 April 2005, but only for the States that have ratified it.

questions.question: What is the key rule governing the scope of the additional protocols?
choices: A protocol binds every Member State of the Council of Europe as soon as it comes into force
A protocol binds only the States that voted in favour of it within the Committee of Ministers
A protocol binds a State as soon as that State has signed it, whether or not it has ratified it
A protocol binds only the States that have ratified it, whereas the Convention rights apply to all States parties
questions.explanation: The course's example: Turkey and Protocol 13, on the basis that a State that has not ratified is not bound by the total abolition of the death penalty.
questions.source: CM Anglais, protocols ; Plan II.B
questions.flag: Careful: the example is out of date. Turkey ratified Protocol 13 in 2006. Azerbaijan is now the only member State not to have ratified it. The principle itself is unaffected.

questions.question: In the language of the Convention, a 'protocol' is:
choices: A reservation entered by a State upon signature
A decision of the Committee of Ministers enforcing a judgment
A procedural rule governing hearings before the Court
An amendment or addition to a treaty or convention
questions.explanation: Glossary definition. Protocols added new rights over time: private property, education, freedom of movement, free elections.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Glossary

questions.question: An 'absolute right' is:
choices: A right that can be enforced exclusively by the European Court of Human Rights
A right regarding which no derogation is allowed
A right which can be interfered with or derogated from under limited circumstances to protect specific public interests
A right belonging only to the nationals of the Member States that did not opt out of articles 3, 4 and 7
questions.explanation: Absolute (or unqualified) rights cannot be derogated from under any circumstances, not even in time of war. The wording about interference under limited circumstances to protect specific public interests is the definition of a QUALIFIED right, which is the trap. This is annales Question 6.
questions.source: CM Anglais, The nature of rights ; Plan III ; QCM ANGLAIS Q6

questions.question: A 'qualified right' is:
choices: A right which no State may ever restrict
A right contained in a protocol rather than in the Convention itself
A right which may only be invoked together with another Convention right
A right which may be interfered with or derogated from under limited circumstances in order to protect certain public interests, provided the interference is necessary and proportionate
questions.explanation: Beware of the wording about a right that may only be invoked together with another right: that describes article 14, which is non-autonomous, a different notion altogether.
questions.source: CM Anglais, The nature of rights ; Plan III

questions.question: According to the course plan, which articles are classified as absolute or unqualified rights?
choices: Articles 2, 3, 4 and 7
Articles 2, 3, 6 and 13
Articles 3, 5, 6 and 7
Articles 8, 10, 11 and Protocol 1 article 1
questions.explanation: Right to life, prohibition of torture, prohibition of slavery, no punishment without law. Note the lecturer's caveat: article 2 is presented as absolute even though the text itself provides for exceptions.
questions.source: CM Anglais, The nature of rights ; Plan III
questions.flag: The printed handout lists only articles 3, 4(1) and 7 as absolute. The lecture notes and the course plan add article 2. Follow the plan: 2, 3, 4, 7.

questions.question: According to the course plan, which of the following sets are qualified rights?
choices: Articles 8, 10, 11 and Protocol 1 article 1
Articles 2, 3, 4 and 7
Articles 5, 6, 13 and 14
Articles 1, 12, 15 and 16
questions.explanation: Private and family life, freedom of expression, freedom of assembly, protection of property. The handout also includes article 9 in this list.
questions.source: CM Anglais, The nature of rights ; Plan III

questions.question: The 'two-tier test' applied by the Court to a State's interference with a qualified right consists in asking:
choices: First, whether the interference serves a legitimate aim; second, whether it was necessary and proportionate
First, whether the interference was provided for by law; second, whether compensation was paid
First, whether domestic remedies were exhausted; second, whether the application was lodged in time
First, whether the right at issue is absolute; second, whether the State has ratified the relevant protocol
questions.explanation: Worked example from the lecture: deporting an undocumented foreign national always pursues a legitimate aim (fighting illegal immigration), but proportionality depends on the strength of the person's family ties in the country.
questions.source: CM Anglais, The nature of rights ; Plan III

questions.question: Regarding the protection of Convention rights, the notion of 'proportionality' refers to:
choices: The possibility for a State to interfere with one or several QUALIFIED rights provided that the interference is necessary and proportionate to a legitimate aim
The possibility for a State to interfere with any Convention right, whether qualified or absolute, provided that the interference is necessary and proportionate to a legitimate aim
The fact that it is never possible for a State to interfere with any right protected by the Convention, since rights are inherent to everyone
The possibility for a State to interfere with one or several ABSOLUTE rights provided that the interference is necessary and proportionate to a legitimate aim
questions.explanation: Proportionality applies to qualified rights only. There is no proportionality analysis for an absolute right: any interference is a violation. This is annales Question 8.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Principle of proportionality ; Plan V.A ; QCM ANGLAIS Q8

questions.question: Under article 15 of the Convention, which rights may NEVER be derogated from even in time of war or other public emergency?
choices: The right to a fair trial, the right to liberty and the right to an effective remedy
Freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and freedom of religion
Freedom from torture, freedom from slavery and no punishment without law
All the rights contained in the Convention and its protocols
questions.explanation: Articles 3, 4 and 7 in the handout's list. Derogation also requires a real public emergency threatening the life of the nation and that the State set out the rights it intends to limit and the oversight mechanisms envisaged.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 15

questions.question: In the glossary of the course, 'derogation or reservation' means:
choices: The refusal of a State to execute a judgment of the Court
Non-application or non-acceptance of part of a treaty or convention, usually for a limited period of time
The withdrawal of a State from the Council of Europe
A decision by the Court not to examine an application on the merits
questions.explanation: Glossary definition.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Glossary

questions.question: Article 2 imposes on the State:
choices: An obligation to refrain from intentionally and unlawfully taking someone's life AND an obligation to safeguard the lives of people within its jurisdiction
Only an obligation to prosecute those who unlawfully take a life
An obligation to abolish the death penalty in all circumstances
Only an obligation to refrain from intentionally and unlawfully taking someone's life
questions.explanation: Article 2 has a negative limb (do not kill) and a positive limb (introduce laws and criminal penalties protecting life). Abolition of the death penalty comes from Protocols 6 and 13, not from article 2.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article II ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 2

questions.question: Under article 2, deprivation of life does NOT contravene the Convention when it results from the use of force which is no more than absolutely necessary. Which of the following is NOT one of the situations listed?
choices: In order to carry out a death sentence lawfully imposed by a court
When acting lawfully to prevent a riot
In order to effect a lawful arrest or prevent the escape of a person lawfully detained
In defence of any person from unlawful violence
questions.explanation: The three listed situations are: defence against unlawful violence, lawful arrest or prevention of escape, and quelling a riot. Execution of a death sentence is dealt with by Protocols 6 and 13, not by this list.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article II ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 2

questions.question: Where a suspicious death occurs, article 2 has been interpreted as requiring the State to:
choices: Investigate the death properly
Refer the matter to the European Court of Human Rights
Compensate the family of the deceased automatically
Prosecute the person suspected of causing the death
questions.explanation: This is the procedural limb of article 2.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article II ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 2

questions.question: In Kontrová v Slovakia [2007], the Court found a violation of article 2 because:
choices: Slovak police officers had themselves used lethal force against the applicant's children

The police had failed to pursue reported incidents of domestic violence and thereby failed to take appropriate positive action to protect the lives of the applicant's children, who were later murdered by her husband
Slovakia had not made domestic violence a criminal offence
Slovakia had failed to investigate the deaths after they occurred
questions.explanation: The case is the course's illustration of positive obligations under article 2: the State's liability arises from the authorities' inaction.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article II ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 2

questions.question: Article 3 provides that no one shall be subjected to torture or to inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. This prohibition:
choices: May be derogated from in times of war or public emergency threatening the life of the nation
Applies only to acts committed by State agents, never to omissions
May be restricted where necessary in the interests of national security
Is absolute and may not be derogated from, even in times of war or public emergency
questions.explanation: Article 3 is the archetypal absolute right, and it can be violated by omission as well (see Z v UK).
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article III ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 3

questions.question: How does the Court determine whether conduct amounts to torture, to inhuman treatment or to degrading treatment?
choices: It applies a 'severity test': ill-treatment must pass a minimum level of severity, and the distinction between the three is a matter of degree
It relies on the classification adopted by the domestic courts of the respondent State
It applies the margin of appreciation, leaving each State to define the three notions
It applies a proportionality test, weighing the treatment against the aim pursued by the authorities
questions.explanation: The difference between torture and inhuman or degrading treatment is one of degree, assessed under the severity test. No proportionality reasoning applies: article 3 is absolute.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article III ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 3

questions.question: In Ireland v UK [1978], the Court held that the five sensory deprivation and disorientation techniques used by the British authorities in Northern Ireland amounted to:
choices: A violation of article 5 only, the detention itself being unlawful
Inhuman and degrading treatment, but not torture, as they were not at the time considered severe enough
No violation of article 3, since the persons detained were suspected IRA members
Torture
questions.explanation: A violation of article 3 was found against the UK, but the treatment was classified as inhuman and degrading rather than torture. This is annales Question 12, where the correct answer is precisely 'inhuman and degrading treatment'.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article III ; QCM ANGLAIS Q12

questions.question: What made Ireland v UK [1978] procedurally remarkable?
choices: It was the first case in which a State was ordered to amend its Constitution
It was the first inter-State case brought before the European Court of Human Rights
It was the first case decided by the Grand Chamber
It was the first case in which the Court awarded just satisfaction
questions.explanation: Inter-State cases are rare but usually significant. Note that a State may bring a case against another State, which disposes of the annales Question 12 distractor claiming that inter-State applications are impossible.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article III ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 3

questions.question: Which techniques were at issue in Ireland v UK [1978]?
choices: Prolonged solitary confinement in an unlit cell
Forced labour in a high-security prison
Electric shocks and beatings during interrogation
Sleep deprivation, exposure to permanent noise, and withholding of food and drink
questions.explanation: Five sensory deprivation and disorientation techniques used in places of detention in Northern Ireland against IRA members.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article III ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 3

questions.question: In Z v UK [2001], the Court found a violation of article 3 because:
choices: The complexity of High Court procedure had made self-representation ineffective in practice
A Local Authority had failed to remove four children from their mother even though it was aware that they were subjected to an unacceptable level of abuse and neglect over four years
A journalist had been fined for contempt of court for refusing to reveal the identity of a whistleblower
Two soldiers had been investigated and dismissed from the armed forces because of their homosexuality
questions.explanation: Z v UK is the course's illustration that article 3 can be violated by omission. This scenario is annales Question 17.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article III ; QCM ANGLAIS Q17

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four types of work excluded from the notion of forced or compulsory labour under article 4?
choices: Work done during legitimate detention or on conditional release
Work performed under an ordinary employment contract at below the minimum wage
Compulsory military service
Community service in a public emergency
questions.explanation: The four exclusions are: work during legitimate detention or conditional release, compulsory military service, community service in a public emergency, and any work forming part of normal civic obligations.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article IV ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 4

questions.question: In the course example, doctors and pharmacists required by their professional body to be on duty at night and at weekends argued this amounted to forced labour. The Court:
choices: Found a violation of article 4, since the obligation was imposed without consent
Dismissed the case, holding that this was work forming part of a normal civic obligation
Found a violation of article 4 combined with article 14
Held the application inadmissible because professional obligations fall outside the Convention
questions.explanation: 'Normal civic obligation' is the fourth exclusion listed by article 4.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article IV

questions.question: In Siliadin v France [2005], the Court found a violation of article 4 because:
choices: France had itself subjected the applicant to forced labour through a public authority
France had required the applicant to perform community service in a public emergency
France had refused to grant the applicant a residence permit
French criminal legislation at the time had failed to protect a 15-year-old girl, brought from Togo and made to work 15 hours a day, seven days a week, without pay, from servitude
questions.explanation: The violation lay in the inadequacy of the criminal law to protect her, a positive obligation, and the perpetrators were private individuals.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 4

questions.question: Article 5 provides that an arrest or detention is lawful only if it falls within one of:
choices: Three permitted grounds exhaustively listed
Four permitted grounds exhaustively listed
Six permitted grounds exhaustively listed
An open list of grounds, provided the detention is proportionate
questions.explanation: Six grounds. This figure is very QCM-friendly.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article V ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 5

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the six permitted grounds of detention under article 5?
choices: To prevent a person from expressing opinions that threaten public order
To prevent unauthorised entry into a country of a person who has been deported or extradited
Failure to obey a court order
Conviction by a competent criminal court
questions.explanation: The six grounds: conviction by a criminal court; failure to obey a court order; ensuring attendance at court where there is reasonable suspicion of an offence; educational supervision of a minor or to bring a minor before a court; persons of unsound mind, alcoholics, addicts, vagrants or carriers of infectious diseases; preventing unauthorised entry or securing deportation or extradition.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article V ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 5

questions.question: Under article 5, a person may be detained on the ground of unsound mind, alcoholism or addiction, or:
choices: Because they have refused to pay a private debt
Because they are a foreign national without documentation
Because they carry an infectious disease
Because they have refused medical treatment
questions.explanation: The ground covers persons of unsound mind, alcoholics, addicts, vagrants and carriers of infectious diseases. The course notes the British authorities' use of this ground against people with AIDS in the 1980s. Note that the prohibition of imprisonment for debt is a separate matter, dealt with by Protocol 4 article 1.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article V ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 5

questions.question: Even where an arrest or detention falls within one of the six permitted grounds, the Court may still find a violation of article 5 if:
choices: The detention lasted more than six months
The deprivation of liberty is considered unreasonable
The person detained is a foreign national
The person was not assisted by a lawyer during the arrest
questions.explanation: Lawful ground and reasonableness are cumulative requirements, as DG v Ireland illustrates.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article V ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 5

questions.question: In DG v Ireland [2002], the Court found a violation of article 5 because:
choices: A minor who should have been placed in a secure educational facility was detained in an institution for young offenders, which is not lawful detention for the purposes of educational supervision
A minor had been detained without ever being brought before a court
A minor had been detained solely because he was considered a danger to himself
A minor had been detained for longer than the maximum period permitted by Irish law
questions.explanation: The ground itself (educational supervision of a minor) was available, but the place of detention did not match it, so the detention was outside the article.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article V ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 5

questions.question: Which Convention article generates more cases before the European Court of Human Rights than any other?
choices: Article 13
Article 8
Article 6
Article 3
questions.explanation: The right to a fair trial, in both criminal and civil cases.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article VI ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 6

questions.question: Article 6 entitles everyone to:
choices: A hearing before a court of the same nationality as the accused
A fair and public hearing before a court composed exclusively of professional judges
A fair and public hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial body established by law
A hearing within six months of the charge being brought
questions.explanation: Independence, impartiality, a legal basis, publicity and reasonable time are the structural requirements.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article VI ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 6

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT among the minimum rights of a person charged with a criminal offence under article 6?
choices: The right to be released on bail pending trial
The right to be informed promptly of the charges in a language he or she understands
The right to have time and facilities to prepare a defence
The right to have witnesses examined
questions.explanation: The minimum rights listed are: information on the charges in an understandable language, time and facilities to prepare a defence, self-defence or legal assistance, examination of witnesses, and an interpreter if required. Pre-trial release is dealt with under article 5.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article VI ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 6

questions.question: Why did the Court hold that the French 'procureur de la République' is not an independent authority for the purposes of article 6?
choices: Because he is appointed by the Conseil supérieur de la magistrature
Because he represents the interests of the victim
Because he is not a professional judge
Because he takes orders from the government, which is why the decision to extend police custody now falls to the juge des libertés et de la détention
questions.explanation: A textbook example of the Convention's direct effect on French criminal procedure.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article VI ; Plan IV

questions.question: In Airey v Ireland [1979], the Court found a violation of article 6 because:
choices: Legal aid was available only in criminal cases, so the applicant could not afford the lawyer she needed in practice to obtain a judicial separation, leaving her without effective access to a court
The Irish courts had refused to grant the applicant a divorce
The proceedings had lasted an unreasonably long time
The applicant had been denied the assistance of an interpreter
questions.explanation: A right that exists only on paper is not an effective right. Ireland introduced civil legal aid as a result. Careful: annales Question 18 uses this very scenario as a distractor, the right answer there being Open Door and not Airey.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article VI ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 6

questions.question: In Tsfayo v UK, the Court found a violation of article 6-1 because:
choices: The Housing Benefits Review Board that heard the applicant's appeal was not independent of the Council whose decision was challenged, nor impartial in its processes
The proceedings before the High Court had lasted more than five years
The applicant, an Ethiopian national, had been discriminated against on grounds of nationality
The applicant had been denied legal aid
questions.explanation: The structural point is the same as in Chahal under article 13: the reviewing body must be independent of the body whose decision is challenged.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 6
questions.flag: The handout dates this case 2007; the judgment was in fact delivered on 14 November 2006.

questions.question: The course explains that French law was changed to allow the assistance of a lawyer in police custody following a judgment delivered against:
choices: France itself
The United Kingdom
Belgium
Turkey, whose legislation was the same as French law at the time
questions.explanation: This is the course's key illustration of why one must rely on the Court's case law against other States, not only against the respondent State.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article VI and Subsidiarity ; Plan IV and VI.A

questions.question: The principle of 'no punishment without law' under article 7:
choices: Prevents a State from sentencing a person who was refused legal assistance during police questioning
Prevents a State from convicting someone of a crime for an act that was not a crime at the time it was committed
Prevents a State from enacting civil or criminal laws that would have any retroactive effect
Prevents a State from increasing OR reducing a penalty retrospectively
questions.explanation: Three traps here. Article 7 concerns criminal law, not civil law; a retroactive REDUCTION of the penalty is permitted (rétroactivité in mitius); and the lawyer in custody is an article 6 issue. This is annales Question 10.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article VII ; Plan IV ; QCM ANGLAIS Q10

questions.question: A person commits an offence at a time when the maximum sentence is two years. Before trial, the law is changed and the maximum becomes three years. Under article 7:
choices: The new law applies, so the maximum becomes three years
The new law applies only if the accused consents
The court may choose between the two laws
Only the old law can be applied, so the maximum remains two years
questions.explanation: The reverse is permitted: if the new maximum were one year, the more lenient new law could be applied. That is the retroactivity in mitius the course insists on.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article VII ; Plan IV

questions.question: Article 7 is also said to ensure the principle of legal certainty, which means that:
choices: A person may not be tried twice for the same facts
The law must be published in the official journal before it enters into force
Criminal proceedings must be concluded within a reasonable time
The law can be used as a basis for punishability only if it clearly describes the criminal behaviour and its consequences
questions.explanation: The clearer the definition of the offence, the less scope for divergent interpretations. Non bis in idem belongs to Protocol 7 article 4.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article VII ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 7

questions.question: In Kononov v Latvia [2010], the Court held that the applicant's conviction did NOT violate article 7 because:
choices: Latvia had entered a reservation to article 7
The acts of which he was convicted constituted a crime under international law at the time they were committed, even though they were not an offence in Latvian domestic law
War crimes are excluded from the scope of article 7
The applicant had waived his article 7 rights by pleading guilty
questions.explanation: Acts committed as a soldier in the Soviet Army during the Second World War. The reference point for legality under article 7 is not only domestic law.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article VII ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 7

questions.question: Under article 8, an interference by a public authority with the right to respect for private and family life is permissible where:
choices: The interference pursues one of the aims listed in the article, whether or not it is proportionate
The interference is in accordance with the law, pursues one of the aims listed in the article, and is proportionate
Never: article 8 admits of no interference whatsoever
The interference is in accordance with the law, whether or not it pursues a legitimate aim
questions.explanation: Article 8 is a qualified right: legality, legitimate aim AND proportionality are cumulative. Any answer dropping proportionality is wrong. Annales Question 7 is built on exactly this point.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article VIII ; Plan IV ; QCM ANGLAIS Q7

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the grounds on which article 8 may be restricted?
choices: To prevent disorder or crime
To protect health or morals
To preserve the cultural identity of the nation
For the economic well-being of the country
questions.explanation: The six listed grounds are: national security, public safety, the economic well-being of the country, the prevention of disorder or crime, the protection of health or morals, and the protection of the rights and freedoms of others.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article VIII ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 8 ; Plan IV

questions.question: Article 8 has also been interpreted as meaning that:
choices: The State must compensate any interference with private life, even a proportionate one
Where decisions are taken which will affect a person's privacy or family life, that person must generally be involved in the decision-making process
Private life is protected only within the home
Every interference with private life must be authorised by a judge beforehand
questions.explanation: A procedural dimension read into a substantive right.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 8

questions.question: The case brought against the United Kingdom by Jeff Dudgeon established that:
choices: Homosexual couples have a right to marry under article 12
Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation is prohibited by article 14 alone
The dismissal of homosexual soldiers from the armed forces violates article 8
Homosexuality falls within the scope of private life, which reversed the earlier position under which laws prohibiting homosexuality were justified by the protection of health and morals
questions.explanation: This decriminalised homosexuality in Northern Ireland (England and Wales had already done so in 1967); Ireland followed with Norris (1988) and Cyprus with Modinos.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article VIII ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 8 ; Plan IV
questions.flag: Course materials date Dudgeon 1982; the judgment was delivered on 22 October 1981. The handout also dates Modinos v Cyprus 1994, whereas it was 22 April 1993, and Kokkinakis 1994, whereas it was 25 May 1993.

questions.question: Fadeyeva v Russia [2005] shows that article 8:
choices: Protects the confidentiality of medical data transferred between public authorities
Has been applied in environmental matters, imposing an obligation on the State to protect individuals from the impact of living near a polluting industry
Protects Travellers from summary eviction from local authority sites
Protects a father's right to be involved in the adoption process of his child
questions.explanation: Article 8 has been read as imposing an obligation on the State to protect individuals from the impact of living near a polluting industry. Do not confuse it with the transfer of confidential medical data (MS v Sweden), the summary eviction of a Traveller family (Connors v UK) or a father's involvement in the adoption of his child (Keegan v Ireland).
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 8

questions.question: In Connors v UK [2004], the Court found a violation of article 8 because:
choices: The applicant's home was searched without a warrant
A Traveller family was refused permission to settle on a site of their choosing
A Traveller family was evicted from a local authority site by a summary procedure, with no justification offered and no possibility of challenge before the courts
The applicant was denied social housing on grounds of ethnicity
questions.explanation: The Court held that the position of Travellers as a minority requires special consideration of their needs and way of life, both in the regulatory framework and in decision-making.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 8

questions.question: According to the course, the notion of 'family life' under article 8 is broad and includes:
choices: The relationship between an unmarried couple, and a father's right to be involved in the adoption process of his child
Only relationships involving a minor child
Only relationships recognised as such by the domestic law of the respondent State
Only relationships between married spouses and their legitimate children
questions.explanation: Johnston v Ireland for the unmarried couple, Keegan v Ireland (1994) for the father and the adoption process.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 8

questions.question: Article 9 is structured in two parts. The second part provides that freedom of thought, conscience and religion:
choices: May never be restricted, since it is an absolute right
May be restricted only in very limited circumstances, such as in the interests of public safety or to protect the rights and freedoms of others
May be restricted at the discretion of each State under its margin of appreciation
May be restricted only in time of war or public emergency
questions.explanation: Both article 9 and article 10 share this two-part structure: the right, then the permitted restrictions.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article IX ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 9 ; Plan IV

questions.question: Kokkinakis v Greece is remarkable because:
choices: It was the first time the Court found a violation of article 9, in the case of a Jehovah's Witness convicted for proselytism
It was the first case brought by a religious organisation rather than an individual
It was the first inter-State case concerning freedom of religion
It was the first case in which the Court applied the margin of appreciation
questions.explanation: Greece could not show that the conviction was justified in the interests of public safety.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 9
questions.flag: The handout dates this case 1994; the judgment was delivered on 25 May 1993.

questions.question: Which of the following is a ground on which freedom of expression may be restricted under article 10, according to the course?
choices: Preventing the disclosure of information received in confidence
Preserving the economic well-being of the country
Protecting the reputation of the government
Protecting national cultural heritage
questions.explanation: The listed grounds are public safety, the prevention of crime, the protection of health or morals, the protection of the rights of others, and preventing the disclosure of information received in confidence. The last of these is, as the lecturer notes, a protection for lawyers. Beware: 'economic well-being of the country' belongs to article 8, not article 10.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article X ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 10 ; Plan IV

questions.question: In Open Door Counselling Ltd and Dublin Well Woman Centre v Ireland [1992], the Court held that Ireland had violated article 10 because:
choices: Ireland had prohibited abortion altogether
Ireland had denied the applicants access to a court to challenge the injunction
An injunction prevented the applicants from providing information on abortion services legally available in other countries, which was disproportionate to the aims pursued
Ireland had prosecuted the applicants for contempt of court
questions.explanation: The Court's reasoning is proportionality-based: Ireland could limit the information, but not prevent it entirely. This is annales Question 18.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article X ; QCM ANGLAIS Q18

questions.question: Article 11 protects the right to assemble with others:
choices: In all circumstances, including where the assembly turns violent
Provided the assembly is peaceful, and the right is balanced against the rights of others who wish to use the same space
Only where prior authorisation has been obtained from the authorities
Only where the assembly is organised by a registered association or trade union
questions.explanation: The right entitles people to attend and organise marches so long as they remain peaceful.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article XI ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 11

questions.question: In Wilson and the National Union of Journalists and Others v UK [2002], the Court found a violation of article 11 because:
choices: The UK had refused to recognise a right to strike
The UK had banned a trade union on grounds of national security
The applicant had been dismissed for belonging to a trade union
UK law allowed employers to use financial incentives to encourage employees to surrender their trade union rights
questions.explanation: The employer had offered a 4.5% pay rise to staff signing contracts giving up collective bargaining and union recognition; Mr Wilson refused and was denied the rise.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 11

questions.question: Under article 12, national authorities have some flexibility to place limitations on marriage, such as setting the marriageable age, provided that:
choices: Those rules are identical in all Member States
Those rules apply equally to nationals and foreigners
Those rules are approved by the Committee of Ministers
Those rules never impair the essence of the right to marry
questions.explanation: Regulation is allowed, negation is not.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article XII ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 12 ; Plan IV

questions.question: In Johnston v Ireland, the Court held that:
choices: There was a violation of article 12 and of article 8 in respect of both applicants
The application was inadmissible because divorce falls outside the scope of the Convention
There was a violation of article 12, because the prohibition of divorce made the right to marry ineffective

There was no violation of article 12, because the right to marry does not include the right to divorce, but there was a violation of article 8 on behalf of the couple's daughter, since Irish law failed to respect the family life of a child born outside marriage
questions.explanation: A double-barrelled holding that is ideal QCM material: no violation of article 12, violation of article 8 on account of the daughter's status. Strictly, the Court found the article 8 violation in respect of all three applicants, because of the legal situation of the child born outside marriage.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article XII ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 12 ; Plan IV
questions.flag: Course materials date this case both 1986 and 1987. The judgment was delivered on 18 December 1986.

questions.question: For the purposes of article 13, a remedy is 'effective' only if:
choices: The remedy results in compensation being paid to the applicant
The remedy is available before a court rather than an administrative body
The authority deciding on the remedy is independent of the body said to have violated the right in the first place, and decides within a reasonable time
The remedy suspends the execution of the contested decision in every case
questions.explanation: The mere theoretical possibility of challenging a decision is not enough; the review must be genuine and independent.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article XIII ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 13 ; Plan IV

questions.question: In Chahal v UK [1996], the Court found a violation of article 13 because:
choices: The applicant was deported before his appeal had been heard
The UK had refused to grant the applicant legal aid for his appeal
The applicant had no right of appeal at all against the deportation order

The advisory panel that considered the applicant's appeal against deportation did not offer a fully independent examination of whether his article 3 rights would be at risk if he were deported to India
questions.explanation: Mr Chahal was a Sikh separatist due to be deported on national security grounds. Note the articulation: the article 13 violation concerns the review of an alleged article 3 risk.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article XIII ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 13 ; Plan IV

questions.question: Article 14 is described as 'not a standalone right'. This means that:
choices: It may only be invoked once all the other Convention arguments have failed
The alleged discrimination must fall within the scope of another provision of the Convention, and it must be pleaded together with that other right
It applies only to discrimination by private individuals, not by the State
It may only be invoked by a State against another State
questions.explanation: Protocol 12 would extend this protection into a general, free-standing prohibition of discrimination.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article XIV ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 14 ; Plan IV

questions.question: The expression 'or other status' in article 14 has been interpreted by the Court as covering:
choices: Only economic and social grounds such as property and income
Nothing beyond the grounds expressly listed, which form an exhaustive list
Only grounds recognised as such by the domestic law of the respondent State
Disability, health status and sexual orientation
questions.explanation: The open-ended formula broadens the reach of the article well beyond sex, race, colour, language, religion, opinion, origin, minority association, property and birth.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article XIV ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 14 ; Plan IV

questions.question: In addition to showing that the case falls within the scope of another Convention provision, what must an applicant relying on article 14 demonstrate?
choices: That they belong to a recognised national minority
That the same discrimination has already been condemned by the Court against another State
That they are treated less favourably than others in relation to that right
That the discrimination was intentional on the part of the State
questions.explanation: Comparative less favourable treatment is the core of the test.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 14

questions.question: In 2000, the Court found a violation of article 14 by France on account of the law then applicable in the field of:
choices: Employment law
Property law
Social security law
Inheritance law
questions.explanation: The French rule under which a child born of adultery received only half the share of the other children in a succession. France amended its legislation as a result. This is annales Question 16; the case is Mazurek v France, 1 February 2000.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article XIV ; Plan IV ; QCM ANGLAIS Q16

questions.question: The Belgian Linguistics Case [1968] is significant because:
choices: It was the first case in which the Court found a violation of article 14 taken alone
It was the first inter-State case before the Court
It was the first case in which a State was ordered to change its language legislation
It was the first article 14 case brought before the Court and the first on the right to education, the Court finding a violation of Protocol 1 article 2 in conjunction with article 14
questions.explanation: French-speaking children were denied access to French-speaking schools solely on the basis of their parents' addresses. Note the combination technique: P1-2 taken with article 14.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 14

questions.question: In Larkos v Cyprus [1999], the Court found violations of:
choices: Article 8 and article 14, holding that the State should offer the same protection to all types of tenants
Article 14 taken alone
Article 6 and article 13
Protocol 1 article 1 alone
questions.explanation: A local authority tenant had less security of tenure than a tenant of a private landlord.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Equality and Non-Discrimination

questions.question: The article dealing with the protection of property:
choices: Allows a State to deprive someone of their property without any compensation if it is in the public interest
Prevents a State from depriving someone of their property even if it is in the public interest
Allows a State to deprive someone of their property even if it is not in the public interest, subject to the payment of due compensation
Prevents a State from depriving someone of their property, except if it is in the public interest and subject to the payment of due compensation
questions.explanation: Public interest AND compensation are cumulative. This is annales Question 11.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Protocole 1 article 1 ; QCM ANGLAIS Q11

questions.question: Protocol 1 article 1 is divided into three parts. Which of the following is the third?
choices: Everyone is entitled to the peaceful enjoyment of their possessions
Everyone is entitled to compensation where their property is expropriated
No one may have their possessions taken away except as provided for by law
The provisions may not restrict the State in enforcing laws necessary to control the use of property or to secure the payment of taxes or other charges
questions.explanation: The third limb is what saves tax measures, as the course's example of the tax on vacant dwellings in Montpellier illustrates.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Protocole 1 article 1 ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Protocol 1 Article 1 ; Plan IV

questions.question: An owner leaves a flat empty in a city under housing pressure and is taxed on the vacant dwelling. He complains of a violation of Protocol 1 article 1. According to the course, the Court's answer is that:
choices: There is a violation, unless the State pays compensation equal to the lost rent
There is a violation, because the owner may do as he wishes with what he owns
There is no violation, because the article does not restrict the State in enforcing laws necessary to control the use of property or to secure the payment of taxes
The complaint is inadmissible, because taxation falls outside the scope of the Convention
questions.explanation: The third limb of P1-1 covers control of use and taxation. Montpellier is one of the French cities concerned.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Protocole 1 article 1 ; Plan IV

questions.question: In Dokic v Bosnia and Herzegovina [2010], the Court found a violation of Protocol 1 article 1 because:
choices: The applicant's flat had been destroyed during the war without compensation
The applicant was treated differently from others on the basis of his Serbian ethnicity when seeking to repossess his pre-war home
The applicant's property had been expropriated without any legal basis
The applicant had been taxed on a property he no longer occupied
questions.explanation: A lecturer at a military school who had vacated his Sarajevo flat during the 1992-1995 war and was refused repossession afterwards.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Protocol 1 Article 1
questions.flag: The course handout attributes the violation to a difference in treatment based on the applicant's Serbian ethnicity. The Court in fact found a disproportionate interference with the peaceful enjoyment of possessions (no repossession and no compensation) and did not examine article 14 separately.

questions.question: How many judges sit on the European Court of Human Rights?
choices: 46, one per Member State of the Council of Europe
27, one per Member State of the European Union
17, the members of the Grand Chamber
7, the members of a Chamber
questions.explanation: One judge per Member State of the Council of Europe. 17 and 7 are the sizes of the Grand Chamber and of a Chamber.
questions.source: CM Anglais, The European Court of Human Rights ; Plan I.B
questions.flag: The printed handout still says 47, before Russia ceased to be a member in 2022.

questions.question: A committee of the European Court of Human Rights is composed of:
choices: Seven judges
A single judge
Three judges
Seventeen judges
questions.explanation: Single judge and three-judge committee for admissibility or for merits already covered by established case law; seven-judge Chamber for other cases; Grand Chamber of 17 for the most serious.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Composition of the Court ; CM ANGLAIS(1), 4.

questions.question: A Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights is composed of:
choices: Three judges
Seventeen judges
Seven judges
Five judges
questions.explanation: Seven-judge Chamber.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Composition of the Court ; CM ANGLAIS(1), 4.

questions.question: The Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights is composed of:
choices: Twenty-one judges
Seven judges
Seventeen judges
Forty-six judges
questions.explanation: 17 judges, for cases raising serious questions or undecided points of law.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Composition of the Court ; CM ANGLAIS(1), 4.

questions.question: Which formation may rule on a case concerning an issue already covered by established case law?
choices: A seven-judge Chamber only
The Grand Chamber only
The plenary Court
A single judge or a three-judge committee
questions.explanation: Established case law is handled by the lightest formations, which is what allows the Court to cope with its caseload.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Composition of the Court ; CM ANGLAIS(1), 4.
questions.flag: As taught. In strict terms a single judge may only declare an application inadmissible or strike it out; only a three-judge committee may rule on the merits of a matter covered by well-established case law (article 28).

questions.question: How is the Grand Chamber composed, according to the course handout?
choices: One judge from each Member State, drawn by lot
The judges of the Chamber that delivered the judgment, plus ten others
The seventeen most senior judges of the Court
The Court's President and Vice-Presidents, the Section Presidents and the national judge, excluding any judge who first examined the case
questions.explanation: The exclusion of the judges who first examined the case is the point most likely to be tested.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), 4.

questions.question: According to the course, how are cases usually considered before the Court?
choices: Through an oral hearing only where the applicant requests one
Through an oral hearing in Strasbourg in every case
In writing, without any need for the applicant or the defending State to appear in Strasbourg, on the basis of the parties' submissions and supporting documents
Through a hearing held in the respondent State
questions.explanation: In exceptional cases going to the Grand Chamber, representatives of the applicant and of the State may attend a hearing. The principle of disclosure must be respected throughout.
questions.source: CM Anglais, How do you take a case to court ; CM ANGLAIS(1), 3.

questions.question: The European Court of Human Rights has the power to hold States accountable for a failure to respect, protect and fulfil Convention rights. In that respect, the Court has the power:
choices: To fine a State in order to sanction it for a violation
To annul national laws or overrule a judgment issued by a national court where these are in breach of the Convention
To find a State responsible for a violation of a Convention right and order it to amend its legislation to make it comply with the Convention
To find a State responsible and compel it to amend its Constitution
questions.explanation: The Court has no power to annul domestic laws or quash domestic judgments; it condemns the State and requires it to redress the violation, including by general measures. Nor does it fine States: just satisfaction compensates the applicant, it does not punish the State. This is annales Question 14.
questions.source: CM Anglais, The European Court of Human Rights ; QCM ANGLAIS Q14
questions.flag: As taught, and as required by annales Question 14. In strict terms the Court's judgments are declaratory: the State chooses the general measures, under the supervision of the Committee of Ministers, except in pilot judgments where the Court indicates them.

questions.question: The notion of 'general measures' refers to:
choices: A change in the domestic legislation of a Member State in order to make it comply with the Convention
Any compensation paid by a Member State in breach of the Convention to the victim of that breach
The request made by a Member State to be allowed temporarily not to apply some Convention rights due to specific circumstances
The general obligation for a Member State to protect and respect human rights
questions.explanation: General measures ensure the violation does not happen again (policy or legislative change); specific measures redress the individual loss (compensation). The wording about a State asking to be allowed temporarily not to apply certain rights describes a derogation under article 15; the wording about a general obligation to protect and respect human rights describes article 1. This is annales Question 4.
questions.source: CM Anglais, When the court makes a judgement ; Plan VI.G ; QCM ANGLAIS Q4

questions.question: The notion of 'specific measures' refers to:
choices: The measures taken by a State to remedy the loss caused to the individual applicant, typically compensation
The amendment of domestic legislation so that the violation does not recur
The measures taken by the Committee of Ministers to enforce a judgment
Interim measures ordered by the Court before it rules on the merits
questions.explanation: Specific for the individual, general for the system. A recurring pair in QCMs.
questions.source: CM Anglais, When the court makes a judgement ; CM ANGLAIS(1), 5.

questions.question: Which body enforces the judgments of the European Court of Human Rights?
choices: The Grand Chamber of the Court
The Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe
The Registry of the Court
The Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe, composed of the Ministers of Foreign Affairs of the Member States or their permanent diplomatic representatives
questions.explanation: The Committee of Ministers is the Council of Europe's decision-making body and monitors the implementation of judgments, both specific and general measures.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), 6.

questions.question: Which of the following changes was NOT presented in the course as a step taken by a State following a judgment of the European Court?
choices: France abolished the death penalty
Ireland introduced legal aid in civil cases
Bulgaria created an alternative to military service for conscientious objectors
The United Kingdom banned corporal punishment in schools
questions.explanation: The examples given are: Airey (civil legal aid in Ireland), Norris (decriminalisation of homosexuality in Ireland), Johnston (equal status for children born inside or outside marriage), Marckx v Belgium, K.A. v Finland (children in foster care), Campbell and Cosans v UK (corporal punishment), Burdov v Russia (Chernobyl victims), Stefanov v Bulgaria (conscientious objectors).
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), 5. Examples

questions.question: Following which judgment did Ireland decriminalise homosexuality?
choices: Norris v Ireland [1988]
Dudgeon v UK [1982]
Modinos v Cyprus [1994]
Johnston v Ireland [1986]
questions.explanation: The sequence is Dudgeon for the UK, then Norris for Ireland, then Modinos for Cyprus.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), 5. Examples and Article 8

questions.question: Marckx v Belgium [1979] led Belgium to:
choices: Create an alternative to compulsory military service
Introduce legal aid in civil cases
Take steps to stop discrimination against children born outside marriage
Abolish corporal punishment in schools
questions.explanation: Part of the same family of cases as Johnston v Ireland and the French adultery-succession case of 2000.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), 5. Examples

questions.question: The proportionality test applied by the Court requires that any restriction satisfies three conditions. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
choices: The restriction must limit the right to the least degree possible
The restriction must be compensated financially
The restriction must have a legitimate aim
The restriction must be clearly connected to achieving that aim
