questions.explanation: Legitimate aim, rational connection, minimal impairment. The lecturer's image: you cannot use a sledgehammer to crack a nut.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Principle of proportionality ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Section 5 ; Plan V.A

questions.question: In MS v Sweden [1997], the Court found no violation of article 8 because:
choices: Medical data does not fall within the scope of private life
Sweden enjoyed a wide margin of appreciation in health matters

The transfer of confidential medical information from one public authority to another, without the patient's consent, was not out of proportion to the legitimate aim of checking the information received from the patient against the clinic's data
The patient had implicitly consented to the transfer by submitting a claim
questions.explanation: The course's leading illustration of the proportionality test, and note the outcome: NO violation.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Principle of proportionality ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Section 5 ; Plan V.A

questions.question: The principle of 'positive obligations' means that:
choices: States must compensate every applicant who suffers a violation
States must incorporate the Convention into their domestic legal order
States must ensure Convention rights are protected in a proactive way, rather than merely refraining from violating them
States must ratify every additional protocol
questions.explanation: Kontrová v Slovakia (article 2), Siliadin v France (article 4) and Öneryildiz v Turkey (article 2) are the course's illustrations.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Positive obligations ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Section 5 ; Plan V.B

questions.question: In Öneryildiz v Turkey [2004], the Court found a violation of article 2 because:
choices: Turkey had allowed residents to settle near a dangerous site despite their own awareness of the risk

The State was under a positive obligation to put in place an administrative and legislative framework protecting against threats to life, and no one had been charged after a methane explosion at a municipal rubbish dump killed several residents
Turkish police officers had used lethal force against demonstrators
Turkey had failed to investigate a suspicious death in police custody
questions.explanation: The case shows that negligence may engage positive obligations: the State must put in place an administrative and legislative framework protecting life and ensure that any threat to it is properly punished. The State's argument that the victims had chosen to live beside the dump was rejected. Note that no one was ultimately held criminally accountable for the loss of life, which the Court treated as part of the violation.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Positive Obligations

questions.question: The 'margin of appreciation' is:
choices: The degree of discretion the Court allows Member States when interpreting the Convention and applying its rights in their own countries
The percentage of just satisfaction a State may withhold
The discretion of the Court to decide which cases it will examine
The time limit within which a State must execute a judgment
questions.explanation: It reflects the diversity of cultural and legal traditions among the Member States, but it never permits a violation of rights.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Glossary and Section 5 ; Plan V.C

questions.question: In which field is the margin of appreciation left to States described as being WIDE?
choices: Discrimination
Taxation
Family life
Prohibition of torture
questions.explanation: Wide on matters of taxation, to allow for different fiscal and administrative structures; much narrower on family life and discrimination. There is no margin at all in respect of absolute rights.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Margin of appreciation ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Section 5 ; Plan V.C

questions.question: In which fields is the margin of appreciation described as being NARROW?
choices: Taxation and fiscal policy
Family life and discrimination
National security and public safety
Education and religion
questions.explanation: Careful with education and religion: Lautsi shows that a wide margin applies there where no European consensus exists.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Margin of appreciation ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Section 5 ; Plan V.C

questions.question: In Lautsi v Italy [2011], concerning crucifixes displayed on classroom walls in State schools, what was the final outcome?
choices: The Grand Chamber overturned the initial finding of a violation, holding that States enjoy a wide margin of appreciation on social or moral issues such as religion and education where there is no European consensus
The Court found a violation of Protocol 1 article 2 taken together with article 9, and Italy removed the crucifixes
The Court found a violation of article 9 alone
The application was declared inadmissible
questions.explanation: The two-stage history matters: a violation at first, then reversal by the Grand Chamber. The initial finding was based on P1-2 (right to education) together with article 9.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Margin of appreciation ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Section 5 ; Plan V.C

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the guiding principles of the Court set out in the course?
choices: Positive obligations
Proportionality
Reciprocity between States parties
Margin of appreciation
questions.explanation: The handout's list is proportionality, positive obligations, margin of appreciation, and equality and non-discrimination.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Section 5 ; Plan V

questions.question: To which category of rights does the proportionality principle apply?
choices: Absolute rights only
All Convention rights without distinction
Only the rights contained in the additional protocols
Qualified rights only
questions.explanation: Where a right is absolute, no interference whatsoever is allowed, so there is nothing to weigh.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Principle of proportionality ; Plan V.A

questions.question: In the context of the European Convention on Human Rights, the principle of subsidiarity means that:
choices: It is only if national courts dismissed the claim on its merits that the claim may be reviewed by the Court
It is only in respect of qualified rights that alleged violations must be brought before national courts first, alleged violations of absolute rights being submitted directly to the Court

It is only if national courts have had the opportunity to consider and redress the alleged violation and failed to provide redress that an application may be made to the European Court of Human Rights
It is only if national courts declared the claim inadmissible that the claim may be reviewed by the Court
questions.explanation: Subsidiarity makes no distinction between absolute and qualified rights, and it is not conditional on the domestic outcome taking a particular form: what matters is that the national courts had the opportunity to redress the violation and did not. This is annales Question 1.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Principle of subsidiarity ; Plan VI.A ; QCM ANGLAIS Q1

questions.question: Before which national courts must a Convention violation be pleaded?
choices: Before all the national courts, including the courts of first instance
Only from the appeal stage of the proceedings
At any time during the proceedings, including before a national Supreme Court for the first time
Only before the national Supreme Court
questions.explanation: The violation must be raised from the outset, at first instance, and pleaded consistently through appeal and before the highest court. This is annales Question 13.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Principle of subsidiarity ; Plan VI.A ; QCM ANGLAIS Q13

questions.question: What does it mean to plead a violation 'substantively'?
choices: To state with specific reference to the applicable Convention articles why there is a violation, rather than merely alleging one in the abstract
To support the violation with expert evidence
To plead the violation before the highest domestic court
To plead the violation in writing rather than orally
questions.explanation: The lecturer's example: it is not enough to claim a violation of article 13 by the French authorities, you must say why.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Principle of subsidiarity ; Plan VI.A

questions.question: Why does the course insist that lawyers should always seek to have the violation established by the national courts?
choices: Because the European Court will only examine violations already found by a national court
Because if a national court finds a violation, a subsequent application to the European Court becomes unnecessary
Because the time limit only starts running once a national court has found a violation
Because the European Court is bound by the findings of the national courts
questions.explanation: The whole architecture rests on national courts being the first line of enforcement.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Principle of subsidiarity ; Plan VI.A

questions.question: Is it mandatory to appeal to the highest domestic court before applying to the European Court of Human Rights?
choices: Yes, without any exception
No, the highest court need only be seised where an absolute right is at stake
In principle yes, otherwise the application risks being declared inadmissible under article 35, but there are two exceptions
No, an application may be lodged as soon as a first-instance court has dismissed the claim
questions.explanation: The two exceptions: where the highest court has already ruled on the point of law at issue (established case law), and where an appeal to the supreme court requires permission (leave to appeal), as in the United Kingdom.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Principle of subsidiarity ; Plan VI.A

questions.question: Which provision of the Convention lays down the requirement that all domestic remedies must have been exhausted?
choices: Article 35
Article 41
Article 13
Article 34
questions.explanation: Article 35 governs admissibility. Article 41 is just satisfaction. Do not confuse article 13 (effective remedy at national level) with article 35 (exhaustion of remedies as a condition of admissibility).
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Substantive aspects of proceedings

questions.question: In a common law country where an appeal to the Supreme Court requires leave to appeal, an applicant who is refused leave:
choices: Must ask the European Court for a waiver of the exhaustion requirement
Is considered not to have exhausted domestic remedies, so the application is inadmissible
Is considered to have exhausted all domestic remedies
Must apply again for leave before turning to the European Court
questions.explanation: A remedy that is not available as of right cannot be held against the applicant. In France, by contrast, the appeal to the Cour de cassation or Conseil d'État is as of right, so it must be used.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Principle of subsidiarity ; Plan VI.A

questions.question: How should the case law of the European Court be relied on before national courts?
choices: By referring exclusively to judgments delivered against the applicant's own State, since only those are binding on it
By referring to precedents concerning the same Convention article, including judgments delivered against other States, not only against the applicant's own State
By referring only to Grand Chamber judgments
National courts are not permitted to take the Court's case law into account
questions.explanation: The course's key illustration is the Turkish judgment on the lawyer in police custody, which led France to change its own legislation. It is especially useful to consider decisions concerning countries with a similar legal system.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Principle of subsidiarity ; Plan VI.A

questions.question: Which of the following would make an application before the European Court of Human Rights inadmissible?
choices: The applicant has not exhausted all the domestic remedies available
There is already established case law on the alleged violation, making a further ruling unnecessary
The applicant is not a national of the defendant State
The applicant was not directly the victim but only the victim's legal representative
questions.explanation: Established case law does not make an application inadmissible: it allows a lighter formation (single judge or committee) to decide it. Nationality is irrelevant, since the Convention applies to everyone within the State's jurisdiction. An official representative may act on behalf of a clearly identified victim. This is annales Question 3.
questions.source: CM Anglais, conditions ; CM ANGLAIS(1), 2. ; QCM ANGLAIS Q3

questions.question: An application lodged by someone who was not the victim of the alleged violation:
choices: Would be dismissed on the merits
Would be inadmissible
Would be admissible where the article allegedly violated protects an absolute right
Would be referred to the relevant national court
questions.explanation: The applicant must be directly and personally the victim. Note the difference between inadmissibility (the Court does not examine the merits at all) and dismissal on the merits. This is annales Question 19.
questions.source: CM Anglais, conditions ; QCM ANGLAIS Q19

questions.question: According to the lecture notes, which exception is mentioned to the rule that the applicant must be directly and personally the victim?
choices: Where the applicant has died during the proceedings
Where the applicant is a non-governmental organisation
Where the violation concerns an absolute right
Where the applicant is a minor
questions.explanation: The lecture notes state it expressly: 'the claimant must be directly and personally the victim of the alleged violation. But, for one exception: when the claimant is a minor.' The handout adds that a complaint may not be made on behalf of another person unless that person is clearly identified as their official representative.
questions.source: CM Anglais, conditions ; CM ANGLAIS(1), 2. ; Plan VI.B

questions.question: Regarding anonymity before the Court:
choices: Anonymity is available only where an absolute right is at stake
No application may be anonymous, but the applicant may ask the Court to preserve their anonymity, including vis-à-vis the respondent State
No application may be anonymous and the Court can never conceal the applicant's identity
Applications may be lodged anonymously in all cases
questions.explanation: Two distinct things: identification of the applicant towards the Court (mandatory) and publicity of that identity (which may be restricted). This explains case names reduced to initials, such as Z v UK, DG v Ireland or MS v Sweden.
questions.source: CM Anglais, conditions ; Plan VI.B
questions.flag: The lecture notes go further and say the respondent State will not know who the applicant is. Under Rule 47 the applicant may ask that their identity not be disclosed TO THE PUBLIC; the respondent State necessarily knows it. Answer as taught, but do not write this in an essay.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a condition of admissibility listed in the course?
choices: The applicant must be represented by a lawyer when lodging the application
All domestic remedies must have been exhausted within the time limit
The complaint may only concern rights contained in the Convention
The case must not have been brought before the European Court of Human Rights previously
questions.explanation: The course does not make legal representation a condition of admissibility; where the applicant does have a lawyer, the authority given to that lawyer must be part of the application form, completed, dated and signed.
questions.source: CM Anglais, conditions ; CM ANGLAIS(1), 2. ; Plan VI.B

questions.question: What remedies are available against a decision of the European Court declaring an application inadmissible?
choices: Regularisation of the application within a week of the decision
None: a decision declaring an application inadmissible is final and cannot be challenged
A new application lodged within a week of the decision
An appeal to the Appeal Chamber of the Court
questions.explanation: There is no Appeal Chamber at the Court. Inadmissibility decisions, and judgments of committees and of the Grand Chamber, cannot be appealed. This is annales Question 15.
questions.source: CM Anglais, The enforcement ; Plan VI.G ; QCM ANGLAIS Q15

questions.question: Can a State bring a case against another State before the European Court of Human Rights?
choices: Yes, but only with the prior authorisation of the Committee of Ministers
No, only individuals may lodge applications
Yes, but only where the two States have made a declaration accepting the Court's jurisdiction for such cases
Yes, inter-State cases are possible though rare, and usually concern important matters
questions.explanation: Ireland v UK [1978] was the first such case.
questions.source: CM Anglais, conditions ; CM ANGLAIS(1), 2.

questions.question: What is the first thing the Court deals with when it receives an application?
choices: The admissibility of the case
The amount of just satisfaction claimed
The merits of the alleged violation
Whether interim measures should be granted
questions.explanation: If the case is inadmissible, the Court will not decide it on the merits, however well founded the complaint might be.
questions.source: CM Anglais, How do you take a case to court

questions.question: According to the course, within what period must an application be lodged with the Court?
choices: Three months from the final domestic decision
Six months from the final domestic decision, or from the date it was notified to the applicant or their lawyer
Four months from the final domestic decision
One year from the final domestic decision
questions.explanation: The course teaches six months. IMPORTANT: since Protocol No. 15 entered into force, the time limit has in fact been four months for final domestic decisions taken on or after 1 February 2022. Answer six months in this exam, but know the real rule.
questions.source: CM Anglais, The time limit ; Plan VI.C
questions.flag: Positive law: the time limit is now FOUR months (Protocol No. 15, applicable since 1 February 2022). The course has not been updated.

questions.question: When the deadline for an application before the European Court falls on a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday:
choices: The deadline is extended by 12 hours on the next working day
The deadline is extended to the next whole working day only where an absolute right is at stake
The deadline is extended to the next whole working day
The deadline is not extended
questions.explanation: The period ends on the last day even if that day is a Saturday, Sunday or public holiday, unlike French procedural law. This is annales Question 20.
questions.source: CM Anglais, The time limit ; Plan VI.C ; QCM ANGLAIS Q20

questions.question: From what point does the time limit for lodging an application run?
choices: From the date the applicant instructed a lawyer
From the date of the final decision of the highest competent national authority, or from the date that decision was notified to the applicant or their lawyer
From the date the first-instance court delivered its decision
From the date the violation occurred
questions.explanation: The starting point is the final domestic decision closing the exhaustion of remedies, or its notification.
questions.source: CM Anglais, The time limit ; Plan VI.C

questions.question: What interrupts the running of the time limit?
choices: Only the lodging of a complete application, with all the relevant documents
Sending the application by e-mail
Sending any letter to the Registry indicating an intention to apply
Sending the application by fax
questions.explanation: Fax and e-mail do not count as lodging an application. This is a classic QCM trap.
questions.source: CM Anglais, The time limit ; Plan VI.C

questions.question: For the purposes of the time limit, what counts?
choices: The date of posting, as evidenced by the postmark
The date the applicant signed the application form
The date the applicant's lawyer was instructed
The receipt of the complete application by the Registry, not the date of sending
questions.explanation: Hence the practical advice: post well in advance by recorded delivery, deliver the application in person, or have it delivered by a bailiff.
questions.source: CM Anglais, The time limit ; Plan VI.C
questions.flag: As taught. Under Rule 47 §6(a) of the Rules of Court as currently in force, the relevant date is the date of DISPATCH (the postmark), not the date of receipt. The course has not been updated on this point.

questions.question: An application is incomplete and is therefore not taken into account by the Court. What can the applicant do?
choices: Nothing: the application is definitively lost
Appeal against the Registry's refusal to register the application
Submit a new application, provided it is still submitted within the time limit
Ask the Registry to regularise the existing application within a week
questions.explanation: The new application enjoys no extension of the time limit, which is why an incomplete application filed at the last minute is fatal.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Notion of sending an application ; Plan VI.D

questions.question: How must an application be lodged with the Court?
choices: By any written means addressed to the Registry, the form being optional
By using the Court's official application form, available on the Court's website, sent by post to the Registry
Through the national ministry of justice, which forwards it to Strasbourg
By e-mail to the Registry, with the original to follow by post
questions.explanation: Failure to provide precise and accurate information on the form may result in the application not being considered.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Notion of sending an application ; Plan VI.D

questions.question: Which of the following documents is NOT listed in the course among those that should be attached to an application?
choices: Copies of the decisions of the national courts
A certificate of nationality of the applicant
Copies of the submissions relied on before the national courts showing that the Convention was raised there
Documents confirming compliance with the time limit, such as the notification of the highest court's decision
questions.explanation: Nationality is irrelevant to the Convention. Other documents may be attached, such as transcripts, medical or other reports, and witness statements.
questions.source: CM Anglais, documents ; Plan VI.D

questions.question: Why does the course insist on attaching the submissions made before the national courts?
choices: Because the Court will not examine any argument that was not made domestically in writing
Because they establish the applicant's nationality and residence
Because judgments do not always address the Convention points of law raised by the lawyers, so the submissions are the proof that the violation was pleaded domestically
Because the Court needs them in order to calculate just satisfaction
questions.explanation: This is the evidential link between subsidiarity and admissibility.
questions.source: CM Anglais, documents ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Substantive aspects

questions.question: Where the applicant is represented, the authority given to the lawyer:
choices: Must be part of the application form and must be completed, dated and signed by the applicant
Is not required, since the Court presumes the lawyer's authority
Must be drawn up by a notary in the applicant's State
Must be sent separately to the Registry within a month of the application
questions.explanation: A formal point that lends itself well to QCM testing.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Substantive aspects

questions.question: Interim measures before the European Court are:
choices: Measures adopted by the Committee of Ministers pending execution of a judgment
Temporary measures ordered before the case is decided on the merits, where waiting for the final decision would make the harm irreparable
Measures taken by the respondent State to redress an individual violation
Measures ordered by the Court to enforce its final judgment
questions.explanation: The course's example: preventing an extradition to a country where the applicant faces the death penalty, before the Court has ruled.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Interim measures ; Plan VI.E

questions.question: Interim measures ordered by the Court are:
choices: Mandatory for the State concerned, but granted only in exceptional cases, mainly concerning extradition and deportation
Merely recommendations that the State is free to follow or not
Mandatory for the State and granted in every case where they are requested
Available only where an absolute right is at stake
questions.explanation: Binding, but exceptional, and concentrated in removal cases.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Interim measures ; Plan VI.E

questions.question: Where a request for interim measures is dismissed:
choices: The applicant may appeal to the Grand Chamber
No appeal is allowed, and the applicant must inform the Court whether the substantive application will be continued
The substantive application is automatically withdrawn
The applicant may lodge a fresh request within a week
questions.explanation: Two cumulative consequences: no remedy against the refusal, and a duty to tell the Court whether the case goes on.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Interim measures ; Plan VI.E

questions.question: A request for interim measures must:
choices: Simply identify the measure sought and the date of the planned removal
Be justified and explain in detail the grounds of the applicant's fears, the nature of the risks alleged and the Convention provisions said to be violated, with the domestic decisions attached
Be supported by a declaration from the applicant's State of origin
Be filed before the domestic remedies have been exhausted
questions.explanation: Detailed justification plus the domestic decisions of the courts and other domestic bodies.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Interim measures ; Plan VI.E

questions.question: Under which article of the Convention does the Court have the power to award just satisfaction?
choices: Article 35
Article 34
Article 41
Article 13
questions.explanation: Article 41. Article 35 concerns admissibility and exhaustion of remedies.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Just satisfaction ; Plan VI.F

questions.question: Just satisfaction may compensate:
choices: Legal costs and expenses only
Non-financial damage only, financial loss being a matter for the national courts
Financial and non-financial damage, such as mental or physical suffering, as well as legal costs and expenses
Financial damage only
questions.explanation: It is equivalent to damages for the injured party.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Just satisfaction ; Plan VI.F

questions.question: What is the function of just satisfaction?
choices: To punish the State in breach and deter future violations
To fund the execution of general measures by the State
To compensate applicants, not to punish Member States
Both to compensate the applicant and to fine the State
questions.explanation: This compensatory, non-punitive character explains why an application may be declared inadmissible where the applicant has suffered no significant damage. It also disposes of the 'fine the State' distractor in annales Question 14.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Just satisfaction ; Plan VI.F

questions.question: How must a claim for just satisfaction be presented?
choices: Itemised and supported by relevant documents, failing which no award will be made
As a single global figure, which the Court will then adjust
Through the applicant's national authorities
Orally at the hearing before the Chamber
questions.explanation: No itemisation and no supporting documents means no award, however real the violation.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Just satisfaction ; Plan VI.F

questions.question: Can a legal person be awarded just satisfaction?
choices: Only where the legal person is a non-governmental organisation
Yes, for instance for damage to the company's image or uncertainty in planning decisions
Yes, but only for financial loss, never for non-financial damage
No, only natural persons may be compensated
questions.explanation: The Court can award compensation for non-financial loss to a legal person too.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Just satisfaction ; Plan VI.F

questions.question: An application for just satisfaction may be declared inadmissible where:
choices: The violation concerns a qualified rather than an absolute right
The applicant is a legal person rather than a natural person
The Court considers that the applicant has suffered no significant damage
The applicant has already lodged a request for interim measures
questions.explanation: A direct consequence of the compensatory function. Note that a legal person may perfectly well be awarded just satisfaction, for damage to its image for instance.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Just satisfaction ; Plan VI.F

questions.question: Which decisions of the Court cannot be appealed?
choices: Only admissibility decisions
Admissibility decisions and judgments delivered by committees and by the Grand Chamber
All decisions of the Court without exception, including Chamber judgments
Only judgments of the Grand Chamber
questions.explanation: A Chamber judgment is the exception: a party may request that the case be referred to the Grand Chamber for review, though such review is exceptional.
questions.source: CM Anglais, The enforcement ; Plan VI.G

questions.question: A party is dissatisfied with a judgment delivered by a Chamber. What can it do?
choices: Request that the case be referred to the Grand Chamber for review, which is granted exceptionally
Nothing: Chamber judgments are final in all cases
Lodge a new application on the same facts
Appeal to the Committee of Ministers
questions.explanation: It is a referral request, not an appeal as of right.
questions.source: CM Anglais, The enforcement ; Plan VI.G

questions.question: When the Court finds a violation, the respondent State:
choices: Must submit the judgment to its parliament for ratification
Must carry out all the obligations resulting from the judgment and take the steps required to redress the violation, through specific and general measures
Must automatically amend its Constitution
May choose whether or not to execute the judgment, since the Court has no enforcement power
questions.explanation: Judgments are binding on the States concerned; the Committee of Ministers monitors implementation.
questions.source: CM Anglais, When the court makes a judgement ; CM ANGLAIS(1), 6.

questions.question: 'Admissible' means:
choices: Allowed to be heard in court: the case has passed certain technical requirements and will be considered by the court
Accepted by the respondent State
Lodged within the applicable time limit
Well founded on the merits
questions.explanation: Admissibility is a threshold question, entirely separate from whether the complaint is well founded.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Glossary

questions.question: The 'applicant' is:
choices: The judge assigned to examine the case
The person who is bringing a case before a court
The lawyer representing a party before the Court
The State against which a case is brought
questions.explanation: Note the French false friend: 'applicant' is the requérant, not the 'appliquant'.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Glossary

questions.question: 'Binding' signifies:
choices: A procedural formality
A provisional measure
An obligation, or legal duty
A recommendation with no legal force
questions.explanation: Judgments are binding on the States concerned; interim measures are also mandatory for the State.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Glossary

questions.question: 'To contravene' a right means:
choices: To go against or deny a right contained in the Convention
To invoke a right before a national court
To derogate from a right in time of emergency
To restrict a right in a proportionate manner
questions.explanation: A synonym of 'to breach' or 'to violate'.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Glossary

questions.question: A 'domestic remedy' is:
choices: The solutions available to an applicant at national level through national courts, courts of appeal or tribunals
The compensation awarded by the European Court
A remedy provided for by the Convention itself
A remedy available only before the highest national court
questions.explanation: Hence the requirement to 'exhaust domestic remedies' before applying to Strasbourg.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Glossary

questions.question: 'Foreseeability' is:
choices: The requirement that a judgment be executed within a predictable time
The ability of the Court to anticipate the consequences of its own judgments
The obligation on States to plan for public emergencies
The requirement that the law or administrative measure be sufficiently clear and predictable to allow a person reasonably to foresee the outcome of their actions
questions.explanation: Closely connected to the principle of legal certainty under article 7.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Glossary

questions.question: When a convention or treaty is 'in force', this means:
choices: The instrument has been adopted by the Committee of Ministers
The instrument has been signed but not yet ratified
A State has agreed to be bound by the instrument and its provisions now apply
The instrument has been incorporated into domestic law
questions.explanation: The ECHR was written in 1950 and came into force in 1953.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Glossary

questions.question: Rights are said to be 'inherent', which means:
choices: They are entitlements which belong to everyone by virtue of being human
They are enforceable only before an international court
They are granted to individuals by their State
They may never be restricted
questions.explanation: Inherence is why the State does not 'give' rights: it must respect, protect and fulfil them.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Glossary

questions.question: 'Jurisdiction' is defined in the course as:
choices: The territory of a State, strictly defined by its borders
The competence of a national court to hear a given dispute
The extent or territory over which legal or other power extends; it may reach beyond a State's territorial boundaries and includes any activity carried out under the control of the State
The power of the European Court to examine an application
questions.explanation: The extraterritorial element is what made Hirsi Jamaa v Italy possible.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Glossary

questions.question: 'Leave to appeal' means:
choices: The time limit within which an appeal must be lodged
The withdrawal of an appeal by the appellant
The permission that must be obtained from a court, typically a supreme court, before an appeal may be brought
The right to appeal available automatically to any losing party
questions.explanation: Where leave is refused, the applicant is nonetheless treated as having exhausted domestic remedies. In France the appeal to the Cour de cassation or Conseil d'État is as of right, so no leave is needed.
questions.source: CM Anglais, exhaustion of remedies ; Plan VI.A, vocabulary list

questions.question: 'To ratify' means:
choices: That a State signifies its agreement to be legally bound by the terms of a particular convention or treaty
That a State incorporates a treaty into its domestic legislation
That a State signs a treaty at a diplomatic conference
That a State enters a reservation to part of a treaty
questions.explanation: Ratification is what makes a protocol binding on a given State: signature alone is not enough.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Glossary

questions.question: A 'state party' to a convention is:
choices: Any Member State of the Council of Europe
A country against which an application has been lodged
A country that has signed but not ratified the treaty
A country that has agreed to be bound by that treaty and is legally bound by its provisions
questions.explanation: Careful not to confuse 'State party' with 'party to proceedings'.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Glossary

questions.question: A 'provision' is:
choices: The content of a particular article within a law, treaty or convention
A temporary measure ordered by the Court
A condition of admissibility
A sum set aside by a State to pay just satisfaction
questions.explanation: Another false friend to keep in mind alongside 'provisional measures'.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Glossary

questions.question: In the course, 'remedy' primarily means:
choices: The compensation granted by a court
The correction of a procedural irregularity
The possibility of challenging a decision, which under article 13 must also be effective
The execution of a judgment by the respondent State
questions.explanation: The lecturer distinguishes the two possible senses and adopts the first: 'remedy' as the possibility of challenging a decision, rather than as what the judge grants.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article XIII ; Plan VI, vocabulary list

questions.question: 'To uphold a decision' means:
choices: That the court of appeal confirms the decision made by the first court
That the court refers the case back to the first court
That the court of appeal sets aside the decision made by the first court
That the court stays the execution of the decision
questions.explanation: The opposite is 'to reverse a decision'. Note also 'to provide relief', meaning to grant the applicant's claim.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Vocab

questions.question: 'To lodge' or 'to file' an application means:
choices: To publish the application on the Court's website
To submit the application to the Court's Registry
To notify the application to the respondent State
To register the application in a national court
questions.explanation: And only a complete application, received by the Registry, counts as lodged.
questions.source: Plan VI, vocabulary list ; CM Anglais, The time limit

questions.question: 'To redress' a violation means:
choices: To acknowledge publicly that a violation has occurred
To declare an application admissible
To put right the violation, through specific and general measures
To request the referral of a case to the Grand Chamber
questions.explanation: Subsidiarity is expressed precisely in these terms: the national courts must have had the opportunity to consider and redress the alleged violation.
questions.source: Plan VI, vocabulary list ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Substantive aspects

questions.question: In the course's terms, 'Convention', 'covenant', 'treaty' and 'agreement':
choices: Are often used interchangeably to designate a formal international agreement between States
Designate instruments of the Council of Europe, the United Nations, the European Union and the OSCE respectively
Are distinguished by the number of States that have ratified them
Designate four distinct categories of instrument with different legal force
questions.explanation: Glossary definition.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Glossary

questions.question: In the Convention's terminology, the phrase 'rights and freedoms':
choices: Distinguishes the rights in the Convention from those in the protocols
Distinguishes absolute rights from qualified rights
Distinguishes civil and political rights from economic and social rights
Is simply another way of talking about rights
questions.explanation: Glossary definition: 'freedoms' is another way of talking about rights.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Glossary

questions.question: Which pair correctly matches the English term with its French equivalent as given in the course?
choices: Domestic remedy = satisfaction équitable
Interim measures = mesures conservatoires
Just satisfaction = mesures conservatoires
Interim measures = mesures générales
questions.explanation: The course also glosses 'pleadings and submissions' as conclusions or mémoires.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Substantive aspects

questions.question: In the context of the European Convention of Human Rights, the principle of subsidiarity means that:
choices: It is only in respect of qualified rights that alleged violation(s) of the Convention must be brought before national courts first whereas alleged violation(s) of absolute rights can be submitted directly to the European Court of Human Rights
It is only if national courts declared a claim inadmissible regarding the alleged violation(s) of the Convention that the claim at issue can be reviewed by the European Court of Human Rights

It is only if national courts have had the opportunity to consider and redress the alleged violation(s) of the Convention and failed to provide redress that an application may be made to the European Court of Human Rights
It is only if national courts dismissed a claim on its merits regarding the alleged violation(s) of the Convention that the claim at issue can be reviewed by the European Court of Human Rights
questions.explanation: The course's own formulation: 'The principle of subsidiarity requires that national courts must always have the opportunity to consider and to redress the alleged violation of the Convention. It is only if they have not provided redress that an application to the ECHR is possible.' Subsidiarity draws no distinction between absolute and qualified rights, and does not depend on the form the domestic outcome took.
questions.source: QCM ANGLAIS, Question 1 ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Substantive aspects

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct?
choices: Domestic courts are bound by the decisions of the European Court of Human Rights against other States but are totally free to ignore the decisions made against other States
Domestic courts are not bound by the decisions of the European Court of Human Rights and may disregard them entirely
Domestic courts are not bound by the decisions of the European Court of Human Rights but must take them into account

Domestic courts are bound by the decisions of the European Court of Human Rights against their national State and must take into account the decisions made against other States that have a similar legal system
questions.explanation: The course states: 'When a decision is made by a state, only this state is binding by the decision of the ECHR, but this decision should still be the same for the other states', and advises considering decisions concerning 'countries with a similar legal system'. The correct answer reproduces that two-stage structure almost word for word: bound as regards judgments against one's own State, bound to take into account those against States with a similar legal system. The answer saying domestic courts are bound by decisions against other States but free to ignore decisions against other States contradicts itself.
questions.source: QCM ANGLAIS, Question 2 ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Substantive aspects
questions.disputed: The answer stating that domestic courts are not bound but must take the case law into account is the standard UK Human Rights Act formulation, and is defensible if your lecturer taught that ECtHR judgments are declaratory and never bind domestic courts as such. The wording of the course notes points instead to the two-stage answer retained here. Note also that the sujet contains an apparent typo: one distractor says domestic courts are bound by decisions against other States but free to ignore decisions against other States, which is self-contradictory as printed. Worth clarifying in class.

questions.question: Which of the following would make an application before the European Court of Human Rights inadmissible:
choices: There is already established case law by the European Court of Human Rights regarding the alleged violation, hence making it unnecessary for the Court to issue another decision
The applicant is not a national of the defendant State
The applicant has not exhausted all the domestic remedies available
The applicant was not directly the victim of the violation but only the victim's legal representative
questions.explanation: Established case law does not bar an application: it allows a single judge or a three-judge committee to rule on it. An official legal representative of a clearly identified victim may act. Nationality is irrelevant, since the Convention protects everyone within the State's jurisdiction.
questions.source: QCM ANGLAIS, Question 3 ; CM Anglais, conditions

questions.question: The notion of 'general measures' can refer to:
choices: The general obligation for a Member State to protect and respect human rights
Any compensation paid by a Member State that was in breach of the Convention to the victim of the breach
A change in the domestic legislation of a Member State in order to make it comply with the Convention
The request made by a Member State to the Court to be allowed temporarily not to apply all or some of the rights set out in the Convention due to specific circumstances
questions.explanation: General measures prevent recurrence (legislative or policy change); specific measures remedy the individual loss, which is what the answer about compensation paid to the victim describes. The answer about a temporary request not to apply certain rights describes a derogation under article 15; the answer about a general obligation to protect and respect human rights describes article 1.
questions.source: QCM ANGLAIS, Question 4 ; CM Anglais, When the court makes a judgement

questions.question: The fact that the rights set out in the Convention are 'interdependent and indivisible' means that:
choices: All the rights set out in the Convention are of equal value
All the rights set out in the Convention are intertwined and the fact of not respecting one of them may adversely affect another
Everyone is entitled to these rights in equal measure, without discrimination
There must be a violation of at least two rights protected by the Convention for an application to be lodged with the Court
questions.explanation: Glossary definition from the course: 'Rights are linked to each other in such a way that non-observance of one right may impact on another.' The answer about everyone being entitled to these rights in equal measure without discrimination describes universality and non-discrimination, a different idea. Note the risk: 'all rights are of equal value' is the standard gloss of 'indivisible' in Council of Europe glossaries, so it is the most dangerous distractor here. The course's own definition is decisive.
questions.source: QCM ANGLAIS, Question 5 ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Glossary

questions.question: An 'absolute right':
choices: Is a right which can be interfered with or derogated from under limited circumstances to protect specific public interests
Is a right that can be enforced exclusively by the European Court of Human Rights
Is a right regarding which no derogation is allowed
Is a right belonging only to the nationals of the Member States that did not opt out of articles 3, 4 and 7
questions.explanation: The answer describing a right that can be interfered with under limited circumstances to protect specific public interests is the definition of a QUALIFIED right, which is the trap.
questions.source: QCM ANGLAIS, Question 6 ; CM Anglais, The nature of rights

questions.question: The right to Respect for Private and Family Life:
choices: May be interfered with by a public authority if it is in accordance with the law, in the interest of the national security, public safety or prevention of crime or to protect other people's rights and freedoms and if the interference is proportionate

May not be interfered with by a public authority under any circumstances, except in the interest of the national security, public safety or prevention of crime or to protect other people's rights and freedoms, even if the interference is not proportionate
Must not be interfered with by a public authority under any circumstances

Must be interfered with by a public authority if it is in accordance with the law, in the interest of the national security, public safety or prevention of crime or to protect other people's rights and freedoms, even if the interference is not proportionate
questions.explanation: Article 8 is a qualified right: legality, legitimate aim and proportionality are cumulative. Every other option either drops proportionality or turns a faculty ('may') into an obligation ('must').
questions.source: QCM ANGLAIS, Question 7 ; CM Anglais, Article VIII

questions.question: Regarding the protection of the rights guaranteed by the European Convention on Human Rights, the notion of 'proportionality' refers to:
choices: The possibility for a State to interfere with one or several qualified rights protected by the Convention provided that the interference is necessary and proportionate to a legitimate aim to be achieved

The possibility for a State to interfere with one or several absolute rights protected by the Convention provided that the interference is necessary and proportionate to a legitimate aim to be achieved
The fact that it is not possible for a State to interfere with one or several absolute rights protected by the Convention since the rights protected by the Convention are inherent to everyone

The possibility for a State to interfere with one or several rights protected by the Convention, whether qualified or absolute, provided that the interference is necessary and proportionate to a legitimate aim to be achieved
questions.explanation: Proportionality concerns qualified rights only. The answer covering rights 'whether qualified or absolute' is tempting but wrong precisely because it extends the test to absolute rights, where no interference whatsoever is permitted.
questions.source: QCM ANGLAIS, Question 8 ; CM Anglais, Principle of proportionality

questions.question: The interpretation of protocol 13 - article 1 by the European Court of Human Rights is that this article:
choices: Prohibits the death penalty in the Member States in all circumstances except in times of war and in case of treason
Prohibits the death penalty in the Member States but also prevents a Member State from deporting an individual to a country where he/she could face the death penalty
Prohibits the death penalty in the Member States but does not prevent a Member State from deporting an individual to a country where he/she could face the death penalty

Prohibits the death penalty in the Member States but also prevents a Member State from deporting an individual to a country where he/she could face the death penalty except if permission to do so is given by the European Court of Human Rights
questions.explanation: The course states plainly that 'the fact for a member State of the Council of Europe to send someone to a country where a person faces the death penalty is not allowed', which is the basis of the interim-measures example. The answer reserving times of war and treason describes Protocol 6, not Protocol 13; and the Court grants no 'permission' to deport, contrary to what one of the other answers suggests.
questions.source: QCM ANGLAIS, Question 9 ; CM Anglais, protocols and Interim measures

questions.question: The principle of 'No Punishment Without Law' protected by article 7 of the Convention:
choices: Prevents a State from increasing or reducing a penalty or a sentence retrospectively
Prevents a State from enacting civil or criminal laws that would have a retroactive effect
Prevents a State from sentencing an individual who was refused the possibility to get legal assistance during police questioning at the police station or during trial
Prevents a State from convicting someone of a crime for an act that was not a crime at the time it was committed
questions.explanation: Three traps. The answer extending article 7 to 'civil or criminal laws' is wrong because article 7 concerns criminal law only. The answer saying the article prevents 'increasing or reducing' a penalty retrospectively is wrong because a retroactive REDUCTION is permitted (rétroactivité in mitius). The answer about legal assistance during police questioning is an article 6 issue.
questions.source: QCM ANGLAIS, Question 10 ; CM Anglais, Article VII

questions.question: The article dealing with the 'Protection of Property':
choices: Prevents a State from depriving someone of their property even if it is in the public interest
Prevents a State from depriving someone of their property, except if it is in the public interest and subject to the payment of due compensation
Allows a State to deprive someone of their property without any compensation if it is in the public interest
Allows a State to deprive someone of their property even if it is not in the public interest, subject to the payment of due compensation
questions.explanation: Public interest and compensation are cumulative conditions.
questions.source: QCM ANGLAIS, Question 11 ; CM Anglais, Protocole 1 article 1

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding the case Ireland v UK [1978]?
choices: The European Court of Human Rights decided the case against Ireland on the ground that the use of sensory deprivation and disorientation techniques by the British authorities against members of the IRA in places of detention in Northern Ireland was justified by the fact that the IRA was a terrorist group

The European Court of Human Rights decided the case against Ireland on the ground that its application was inadmissible as it was not possible for a Member State to bring a case against another Member State before the European Court of Human Rights
The European Court of Human Rights decided the case against the UK on the ground of the use of inhuman and degrading treatment by the British authorities
The European Court of Human Rights decided the case against the UK on the ground of the use of torture by the British authorities
questions.explanation: A violation of article 3 was found against the UK, but the five techniques were classified as inhuman and degrading treatment, not as torture, as they were not considered severe enough at the time. The answer claiming the application was inadmissible because a State cannot sue another State is doubly wrong: inter-State cases are possible, and this was the first of them.
questions.source: QCM ANGLAIS, Question 12 ; CM Anglais, Article III

questions.question: At what stage of the proceedings should violations of human rights be pleaded?
choices: Only before the national Supreme Court
At any time during the proceedings, including before a national Supreme Court for the first time
Only from the appeal stage of the proceedings
Before all the national Courts, including the Courts of first instance
questions.explanation: The violation must be raised from the outset and pleaded consistently at first instance, on appeal and before the highest court.
questions.source: QCM ANGLAIS, Question 13 ; CM Anglais, Principle of subsidiarity

questions.question: The European Court of Human Rights has the power to hold states accountable for a failure to respect, protect and fulfil the rights contained in the Convention. In that respect, the Court has the power:
choices: To find a State responsible for a violation of a Convention right and compel it to amend its Constitution to make it comply with the convention
To find a State responsible for a violation of a Convention right and order it to amend its legislation to make it comply with the convention
To fine a State to sanction it for a violation
To annul national laws or overrule a judgment issued by a national court if they are in breach of the Convention
questions.explanation: The Court cannot annul a domestic law or quash a domestic judgment, and it does not fine States: just satisfaction compensates the applicant and is expressly not punitive. Amending legislation is the very definition of a general measure.
questions.source: QCM ANGLAIS, Question 14 ; CM Anglais, The European Court of Human Rights

questions.question: What are the remedies available against a decision by the European Court of Human Rights declaring an application inadmissible?
choices: Regularisation, within a week from the decision declaring the inadmissibility
None. A decision declaring an application inadmissible is final and cannot be challenged
Appeal. The decision will be reviewed by the Appeal Chamber of the Court
A new application, lodged within a week from the decision declaring the inadmissibility
questions.explanation: 'If the case is declared inadmissible, there is no remedy = no possibility to appeal.' There is no such thing as an Appeal Chamber at the Court.
questions.source: QCM ANGLAIS, Question 15 ; CM Anglais, How do you take a case to court

questions.question: In 2000, the European Court of Human Rights held that there had been a violation of article 14 of the Convention ('Prohibition of Discrimination') by France due to its then applicable:
choices: Property Law
Social Security Law
Inheritance Law
Employment Law
questions.explanation: The rule under which a child born of adultery received only half the share of the other children in a succession. France amended its legislation afterwards. The case is Mazurek v France, 1 February 2000: the violation was of article 14 taken together with article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The branch of domestic law at issue is inheritance law, which is what the question asks; the Convention hook is the protection of property, which is what makes 'Property Law' the seductive distractor.
questions.source: QCM ANGLAIS, Question 16 ; CM Anglais, Article XIV

questions.question: In the case Z v UK [2001], the European Court of Human Rights considered that:
choices: The UK had violated article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) after two soldiers were investigated and dismissed from the armed forces because of their homosexuality
The UK had violated article 13 (right to an effective remedy) as the complexity of High Court procedure made self-representation ineffective in practice

The UK had violated article 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) by failing to remove four children from their mother as soon as the relevant public authority became aware that they were exposed to terrible neglect and unacceptable emotional abuse
The UK had violated article 10 (freedom of expression) after a journalist was fined for contempt of Court for refusing to reveal the identity of a whistleblower
questions.explanation: Z v UK is the course's illustration that article 3 may be violated by omission: the Local Authority's failure to act over a four-year period. Note that the Court also found a violation of article 13 in this case, so the article 13 distractor is wrong on its facts, not on its article.
questions.source: QCM ANGLAIS, Question 17 ; CM Anglais, Article III

questions.question: In the case Open Door Counselling Ltd and Dublin Well Woman Centre v. Ireland [1992], the European Court of Human Rights considered that:
choices: Ireland had violated articles 6 and 13 as Irish law provided no effective remedy for unjustified delays in criminal proceedings

Ireland had violated article 6 (right to a fair trial) as a woman subjected to violence by her husband was effectively denied access to a court, being unable to obtain a judicial separation for lack of financial resources and legal aid
Ireland had violated article 6 as the applicants' right to remain silent and not to incriminate themselves following their arrest on suspicion of serious terrorist offences had not been respected

Ireland had violated article 10 (freedom of expression) after an injunction prevented the applicants from providing information on abortion services that were legally available in other countries whereas it was illegal in Ireland
questions.explanation: The Court held the injunction disproportionate to the aims pursued: Ireland could limit the information but not prevent it altogether. Note that the answer about the woman unable to obtain a judicial separation for lack of legal aid describes Airey v Ireland [1979], an article 6 case.
questions.source: QCM ANGLAIS, Question 18 ; CM Anglais, Article X

questions.question: An application that would be lodged by someone who was not the victim of an alleged violation of the Convention:
choices: Would be admissible if the Convention article that was allegedly violated deals with an absolute right, as any violation of such a right is so serious that it must be sanctioned irrespective of who is the applicant
Would be inadmissible
Would be referred to the relevant national court
Would be dismissed on the merits
questions.explanation: The applicant must be directly and personally the victim. Watch the distinction with the answer saying the application would be 'dismissed on the merits': the Court would not reach the merits at all, it would declare the application inadmissible.
questions.source: QCM ANGLAIS, Question 19 ; CM Anglais, conditions

questions.question: When the deadline for an application before the European Court of Human Rights falls on a Saturday, a Sunday or a Public Holiday:
choices: The deadline is extended to the next whole working day
The deadline is extended by 12 hours on the next working day
The deadline is extended to the next whole working day only if the alleged violation deals with an absolute right
The deadline is not extended
questions.explanation: 'This period ends on the last day of that period, even if that day falls on a Saturday, a Sunday, or a public holiday (so not the same as in France).'
questions.source: QCM ANGLAIS, Question 20 ; CM Anglais, The time limit

questions.question: What is the difference between article 6 and article 13 of the Convention?
choices: Article 6 applies before national courts and article 13 before the European Court
Article 6 guarantees a fair trial before a court, whereas article 13 guarantees an effective remedy before a national authority, which need not be a court
Article 6 is an absolute right and article 13 a qualified one
Article 6 applies in criminal cases and article 13 in civil cases
questions.explanation: Chahal concerned an advisory panel, Tsfayo a Housing Benefits Review Board: neither was a court, yet both raised the independence issue.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Articles VI and XIII

questions.question: What is the difference between article 13 and article 35 of the Convention?
choices: They are two formulations of the same rule
Article 13 concerns civil remedies and article 35 criminal remedies
Article 13 applies to individuals and article 35 to States
Article 13 creates a substantive right to an effective remedy at national level, whereas article 35 makes the exhaustion of domestic remedies a condition of admissibility before the Court
questions.explanation: One is a right that can itself be violated, the other is a procedural filter.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article XIII ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Substantive aspects

questions.question: Which of these two statements about the death penalty is correct?
choices: Protocol 6 abolishes it with exceptions (war, treason), Protocol 13 abolishes it in all circumstances
Both protocols abolish it in all circumstances, Protocol 13 merely restating Protocol 6
Article 2 of the Convention abolishes it, the protocols merely confirming this
Protocol 6 abolishes it in all circumstances, Protocol 13 abolishes it with exceptions
questions.explanation: 6 comes before 13 in number, but 13 is the stricter of the two. The course adds treason to the Protocol 6 exceptions and cites Turkey as a non-ratifying State: see the flag.
questions.source: CM Anglais, protocols ; Plan II.B
questions.flag: Two inaccuracies carried over from the course. Article 2 of Protocol 6 allows the death penalty only for acts committed in time of war or of imminent threat of war, not for treason. And Turkey did ratify Protocol 13, in 2006.

questions.question: An application is declared inadmissible. What does that mean?
choices: The Court has examined the merits and found no violation
The Court has referred the case back to the national courts
The Court will not examine the merits at all, even if the complaint might well have been justified
The Court has suspended examination pending the exhaustion of domestic remedies
questions.explanation: The lecturer's example: someone convicted without a lawyer or interpreter who applies directly to Strasbourg may be perfectly right on the substance and still lose, because the case is inadmissible.
questions.source: CM Anglais, How do you take a case to court

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a power of the European Court of Human Rights?
choices: Finding a State responsible for a violation
Ordering a State to amend its legislation
Awarding just satisfaction to the victim
Annulling a national law that breaches the Convention
questions.explanation: The Court neither annuls domestic laws nor quashes domestic judgments, and it does not fine States.
questions.source: CM Anglais, The European Court of Human Rights ; QCM ANGLAIS Q14

questions.question: Which of these pairs is correctly matched?
choices: Specific measures = legislative change; general measures = compensation to the individual victim
Specific measures = interim measures; general measures = just satisfaction
Specific measures = compensation to the individual victim; general measures = legislative change
Specific measures = measures ordered by the Court; general measures = measures ordered by the Committee of Ministers
questions.explanation: The single most examinable pair in the procedural part of the course.
questions.source: CM Anglais, When the court makes a judgement ; CM ANGLAIS(1), 5.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes torture from inhuman or degrading treatment under article 3?
choices: The difference is one of degree, assessed by the Court through a severity test
The difference lies in whether the victim suffered lasting physical injury
The difference lies in whether the treatment was intentional
The difference lies in whether the treatment was inflicted by a State agent or by a private individual
questions.explanation: Ireland v UK is the illustration: a violation of article 3 was found, but the threshold of torture was not reached.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article III

questions.question: An applicant complains that a public authority interfered with an absolute right, but argues that the interference was proportionate. How should the Court reason?
choices: The Court refers the question back to the national courts
No proportionality analysis is available: where a right is absolute, any interference amounts to a violation
The Court applies the proportionality test as it would for a qualified right
The Court applies the margin of appreciation to determine whether the interference was acceptable
questions.explanation: This is the structural trap around which several annales questions are built (Q6, Q7, Q8).
questions.source: CM Anglais, Principle of proportionality ; Plan V.A

questions.question: Which of the following statements about inter-State cases is correct?
choices: A State may never bring a case against another State before the Court
A State may bring a case against another State; such cases are rare but usually important
A State may bring a case against another State only with the authorisation of the Committee of Ministers
A State may bring a case against another State only where its own nationals are the victims
questions.explanation: Ireland v UK [1978] was the first, and it concerned treatment inflicted on IRA members, not on Irish nationals as such.
questions.source: CM Anglais, conditions ; CM ANGLAIS(1), 2.

questions.question: Which article was violated in Johnston v Ireland, and which was not?
choices: Article 8 was violated (in respect of the daughter); article 12 was not
Neither article was violated
Both articles 8 and 12 were violated
Article 12 was violated; article 8 was not
questions.explanation: The right to marry does not include a right to divorce, hence no violation of article 12; but Irish law failed to respect the family life of a child born outside marriage, hence a violation of article 8.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article XII ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 12

questions.question: In which of the following cases did the Court find NO violation?
choices: Chahal v UK [1996]
MS v Sweden [1997]
Siliadin v France [2005]
Kontrová v Slovakia [2007]
questions.explanation: MS v Sweden (no violation, proportionate transfer of medical data) and Kononov v Latvia (no violation of article 7) are the two 'no violation' outcomes in the course, alongside the article 12 limb of Johnston and the Grand Chamber's ruling in Lautsi.
questions.source: CM Anglais and CM ANGLAIS(1), case law

questions.question: Which case is correctly matched with its article?
choices: Airey v Ireland / article 11
Kontrová v Slovakia / article 6
Open Door and Well Woman v Ireland / article 9
Kokkinakis v Greece / article 9
questions.explanation: Kokkinakis is the first case in which the Court found a violation of article 9. Kontrová is article 2, Airey article 6, Open Door article 10. Careful with Chahal, which the course classifies under article 13 although the article 3 risk is what the advisory panel failed to examine independently, and with Airey, where the Court also found a violation of article 8.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), case law

questions.question: Which of these case-to-article pairings is correct?
choices: Öneryildiz v Turkey / article 2
Connors v UK / article 11
Wilson and NUJ v UK / article 10
Dokic v Bosnia and Herzegovina / article 8
questions.explanation: Connors is article 8, Wilson is article 11, Dokic is Protocol 1 article 1.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), case law

questions.question: Which case is correctly matched with its subject matter?
choices: Larkos v Cyprus / transfer of confidential medical data
DG v Ireland / failure of the police to act on reports of domestic violence
Kontrová v Slovakia / detention of a minor in a young offenders' institution
Lautsi v Italy / crucifixes in State school classrooms and the margin of appreciation
questions.explanation: Kontrová is the domestic violence case, DG v Ireland the detention of a minor, Larkos v Cyprus the difference in security of tenure between public and private tenants.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), case law

questions.question: Which of the following describes the correct sequence of steps before applying to the European Court of Human Rights?
choices: Raise the violation for the first time before the highest national court, then apply to the Registry
Raise the Convention violation substantively at first instance, plead it consistently on appeal and before the highest court, then lodge a complete application with the Registry within the time limit
Apply to the Committee of Ministers, which will refer the case to the Court
Lodge an application with the Registry as soon as the first-instance court has ruled, then continue the domestic proceedings in parallel
questions.explanation: Subsidiarity, consistency and exhaustion are the three elements running through the whole procedural part.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Principle of subsidiarity ; Plan VI

questions.question: An applicant sends a complete application to the Registry by e-mail on the last day of the time limit. What is the consequence?
choices: The time limit is interrupted, provided the original is posted within a week
The time limit is extended to the next working day
The time limit is not interrupted: an application sent by e-mail or fax does not constitute a valid lodging
The time limit is interrupted, since only the completeness of the application matters
questions.explanation: The course is explicit on this point, and the requirement is receipt by the Registry rather than dispatch.
questions.source: CM Anglais, The time limit ; Plan VI.C
questions.flag: As taught: e-mail and fax do not constitute valid lodging. On the dispatch-versus-receipt question, see the flag on the time-limit questions: the Rules of Court now look to the postmark.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the margin of appreciation is FALSE?
choices: It is narrow on matters involving family life and discrimination
Its extent depends on the nature of the issue before the Court
It allows a State to violate a Convention right where there is no European consensus on the question
It is wide on matters of taxation
questions.explanation: The course states expressly that the margin 'does not permit a violation of rights'. It governs how a State fulfils its obligations, not whether it may breach them.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Margin of appreciation ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Section 5

questions.question: Which of the following statements about article 14 is FALSE?
choices: The list of prohibited grounds is open-ended thanks to the words 'or other status'
Protocol 12 would create a general prohibition of discrimination
The applicant must show less favourable treatment than others in relation to the right at issue
Article 14 may be invoked on its own, independently of any other Convention right
questions.explanation: Article 14 is not a standalone right; it is precisely the limitation that Protocol 12 was designed to overcome.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article XIV ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 14

questions.question: Which of the following is a correct statement about the Convention's territorial scope?
choices: Convention rights apply outside the State's territory only where that State has made a special declaration
Convention rights apply only to nationals of States parties, wherever they may be
Convention rights may apply even where a State operates outside its own territory, wherever the activity is carried out under the control of that State
Convention rights apply only within the land borders of the State party
questions.explanation: The glossary definition of jurisdiction and Hirsi Jamaa v Italy point in the same direction.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Glossary and Article 1

questions.question: In the lecturer's worked example, an undocumented foreign national who has lived in France for twenty years and has three French children is served with a deportation order. How should the article 8 analysis run?
choices: The interference is lawful and therefore no proportionality assessment is required
Article 8 cannot be invoked by a person unlawfully present on the territory
The deportation pursues no legitimate aim, since the person has family ties in France
The deportation pursues a legitimate aim (combating illegal immigration), but the interference with private and family life is disproportionate on these facts
questions.explanation: Compare with the FlixBus variant: a person stopped at the border after five minutes in France has no private or family life there to be affected, so deportation is proportionate. The legitimate aim is constant; proportionality is what varies.
questions.source: CM Anglais, The nature of rights ; Plan III

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the rights contained in the protocols is correct?
choices: They bind only the States that have ratified the protocol in question, whereas the Convention rights bind all States parties
They bind the States that have signed the protocol, whether or not they have ratified it
They bind only the States that have incorporated them into domestic law
They bind every Member State of the Council of Europe without distinction
questions.explanation: A protocol binds only its ratifying States, which is why the abolition of the death penalty in all circumstances does not reach a State that has not ratified Protocol 13.
questions.source: CM Anglais, protocols ; Plan II.B
questions.flag: The course uses Turkey as its example of a State that has not ratified Protocol 13. Turkey ratified it in 2006; Azerbaijan is the correct current example.

questions.question: A judgment is delivered against Turkey concerning the absence of a lawyer during police custody. What conclusion does the course draw for French law?
choices: The judgment binds French courts directly and quashes convictions already handed down
Since French legislation was the same, the same violation would be found against France, which is why France changed its legislation
France would have to wait for a judgment delivered against it before amending its law
The judgment is irrelevant in France, as it was not delivered against France
questions.explanation: This is the practical reason for relying on case law concerning other States, especially those with a similar legal system.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article VI and Principle of subsidiarity

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a consequence of the compensatory, non-punitive function of just satisfaction?
choices: A claim may be declared inadmissible where the applicant suffered no significant damage
The award is equivalent to damages for the injured party
Legal persons may be compensated for damage to their image
The Court may increase the award to deter future violations by the same State
questions.explanation: Just satisfaction is expressly said to compensate applicants, not to punish Member States, so there is no room for a deterrent uplift.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Just satisfaction ; Plan VI.F

questions.question: Which of the following statements about interim measures is FALSE?
choices: Interim measures are mandatory for the State concerned
Where the request is dismissed, the applicant must tell the Court whether the substantive application will continue
Where a request for interim measures is dismissed, the applicant may appeal against that refusal
They are granted only in exceptional cases, mainly concerning extradition and deportation
questions.explanation: No appeal lies against the refusal of interim measures.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Interim measures ; Plan VI.E

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the relationship between article 3 and extradition or deportation, as illustrated by the course?
choices: A State may extradite a person facing such a risk provided it obtains assurances from the receiving State
A State may not send a person to a country where they would face a real risk of treatment contrary to article 3, which is why interim measures are typically sought in removal cases
Article 3 may be derogated from in extradition cases involving terrorism
Article 3 concerns only treatment inflicted on the territory of the respondent State
questions.explanation: The Chahal scenario and the Texas death penalty example both rest on this logic. The course's Texas example shows precisely that assurances given by the receiving authorities may not be trusted.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article XIII and Interim measures

questions.question: Which statement about the Convention and the European Union is correct according to the course?
choices: The Convention is an instrument of the European Union enforced by the Court of Justice
The European Union Charter of Fundamental Rights is enforced by the European Court of Human Rights
The Council of Europe and the European Union share a single court
They are entirely separate systems: the Convention belongs to the Council of Europe and is enforced in Strasbourg, while the EU protects rights through its Charter, enforced in Luxembourg
questions.explanation: The two organisations cooperate but are entirely separate in structure and working methods.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Section 1 ; Plan I.B

questions.question: Under article 15, which condition must be satisfied for a derogation to be valid?
choices: There must be a real public emergency threatening the life of the nation, and the State must set out which rights it intends to limit and what oversight mechanisms will monitor the limitations
The derogation must be limited to a maximum period of six months
The derogation must be authorised in advance by the European Court of Human Rights
The derogation must be approved by a two-thirds majority of the Committee of Ministers
questions.explanation: Derogating measures must also be strictly related to the emergency and must not contradict other rules of international law.
questions.source: CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 15

questions.question: An applicant complains only of a breach of national law, unconnected to any Convention right. The application will be:
choices: Referred to the Court of Justice of the European Union
Examined on the merits and dismissed
Inadmissible, since the complaint can only be about rights contained in the Convention
Admissible, provided domestic remedies have been exhausted
questions.explanation: Ratione materiae: the Court is not a fourth-instance court for domestic law.
questions.source: CM Anglais, conditions ; CM ANGLAIS(1), 2.

questions.question: Which is the correct order of formations, from the lightest to the heaviest?
choices: Single judge, Chamber of five, committee of seven, Grand Chamber of fifteen
Single judge, committee of three, Chamber of seven, Grand Chamber of seventeen
Committee of three, single judge, Chamber of seven, Grand Chamber of seventeen
Committee of three, Chamber of five, Grand Chamber of eleven, plenary Court of forty-six
questions.explanation: 1, 3, 7, 17: a sequence worth memorising as such.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Composition of the Court ; CM ANGLAIS(1), 4.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best summary of what the applicant must prove to succeed under article 13?
choices: That the domestic courts wrongly dismissed the complaint on the merits
That the domestic proceedings lasted more than a reasonable time
That the applicant was denied legal aid in the domestic proceedings
That no effective remedy was available before a national authority independent of the body said to have violated the right, in conjunction with an arguable complaint under another Convention right
questions.explanation: Chahal is the model: the article 13 violation lay in the absence of an independent examination of the article 3 risk.
questions.source: CM Anglais, Article XIII ; CM ANGLAIS(1), Article 13
